unstring: 1. To deprive of a string or strings; also, to take from a string; as, to unstring beads. 2. To loosen the string or strings of; as, to unstring a harp or a bow. 3. To relax the tension of; to loosen. "His garland they unstring." Dryden. Used also figuratively; as, his nerves were unstrung by fear.
unpaganize: To cause to cease to be pagan; to divest of pagan character. Cudworth.
uncreatedness: The quality or state of being uncreated.
understrapper: A petty fellow; an inferior agent; an underling. This was going to the fountain head at once, not applying to the understrappers. Goldsmith.
universalism: The doctrine or belief that all men will be saved, or made happy, in the future state.
untrained: 1. Not trained. Shak. 2. Not trainable; indocile. (old) Herbert.
unintelligence: Absence or lack of intelligence; unwisdom; ignorance. Bp. Hall.
unchurch: 1. To expel, or cause to separate, from a church; to excommunicate. Sir M. Hale. 2. To deprive of the character, privileges, and authority of a church. South.
unreeve: To withdraw, or take out, as a rope from a block, thimble, or the like.
unwormed: Not wormed; not having had the worm, or lytta, under the tongue cut out; -- said of a dog.
unguiculate: 1. Furnished with nails, claws, or hooks; clawed. See the Note under Nail, n., 1. 2. (Bot.) Furnished with a claw, or a narrow stalklike base, as the petals of a carnation.
unseam: To open the seam or seams of; to rip; to cut; to cut open. Shak.
unkingship: The quality or condition of being unkinged; abolition of monarchy. (old) Unkingship was proclaimed, and his majesty's statues thrown down. Evelyn.
unshout: To recall what is done by shouting. (old) Shak.
underreckon: To reckon below what is right or proper; to underrate. Bp. Hall.
untidy: 1. Unseasonable; untimely. (old) "Untidy tales." Piers Plowman. 2. Not tidy or neat; slovenly. -- Un*ti"di*ly, adv. -- Un*ti"di*ness, n.
unyoke: 1. To loose or free from a yoke. "Like youthful steers unyoked, they take their courses." Shak. 2. To part; to disjoin; to disconnect. Shak.
unconcludent: Inconclusive. (old) Locke. -- Un`con*clud"ing*ness, n. (old) Jer. Taylor.
ungovernable: Not governable; not capable of being governed, ruled, or restrained; licentious; wild; unbridled; as, ungovernable passions. -- Un*gov"ern*a*bly, adv. Goldsmith.
underniceness: A want of niceness; indelicacy; impropriety.
universally: In a universal manner; without exception; as, God's laws are universally binding on his creatures.
unlookedfor: Not looked for; unexpected; as, an unlooked-for event.
undecylic: Related to, derived from, or containing, undecyl; specifically, designating that member of the fatty acids which corresponds to undecane, and is obtained as a white crystalline substance, C11H22O2.
underfollow: To follow closely or immediately after. (old) Wyclif.
undying: Not dying; imperishable; unending; immortal; as, the undying souls of men.
undercreep: To creep secretly or privily. (old) Wyclif.
unsoft: Not soft; hard; coarse; rough. (old) "Bristles of his beard unsoft." Chaucer. | Not softly. (old) Great climbers fall unsoft. Spenser.
unmew: To release from confinement or restraint. Keats.
untaste: To deprive of a taste for a thing. Daniel.
untie: 1. To loosen, as something interlaced or knotted; to disengage the parts of; as, to untie a knot. Sacharissa's captive fain Would untie his iron chain. Waller. Her snakes untied, sulphurous waters drink. Pope. 2. To free from fastening or from restraint; to let loose; to unbind. Though you untie the winds, and let them fight Against the churches. Shak.
unruffle: To cease from being ruffled or agitated. Dryden.
unknit: To undo or unravel what is knitted together. Fie, fie! unknit that threatening unkind brow. Shak.
uncharnel: To remove from a charnel house; to raise from the grave; to exhume. Byron.
uninucleated: Possessed of but a single nucleus; as, a uninucleated cell.
unmeet: Not meet or fit; not proper; unbecoming; unsuitable; -- usually followed by for. "Unmeet for a wife." Tennyson. And all unmeet our carpet floors. Emerson. -- Un*meet"ly, adv. -- Un*meet"ness, n.
unshackle: To loose from shackles or bonds; to set free from restraint; to unfetter. Addison.
unite: 1. To put together so as to make one; to join, as two or more constituents, to form a whole; to combine; to connect; to join; to cause to adhere; as, to unite bricks by mortar; | 1. To become one; to be cemented or consolidated; to combine, as by adhesion or mixture; to coalesce; to grow together. 2. To join in an act; to concur; to act in concert;
unreproachable: Not liable to be reproached; irreproachable.
unempirically: Not empirically; without experiment or experience.
unbeliever: 1. One who does not believe; an incredulous person; a doubter; a skeptic. 2. A disbeliever; especially, one who does not believe that the Bible is a divine revelation, and holds that Christ was neither a divine nor a supernatural person; an infidel; a freethinker. Syn. -- See Infidel.
unfurl: To loose from a furled state; to unfold; to expand; to open or spread; as, to unfurl sails; to unfurl a flag.
uncurrent: Not current. Specifically: Not passing in common payment; not receivable at par or full value; as, uncurrent notes. Shak.
undermine: 1. To excavate the earth beneath, or the part of, especially for the purpose of causing to fall or be overthrown; to form a mine under; to sap; as, to undermine a wall. A vast rock undermined from one end to the other, and a highway running through it. Addison. 2. Fig.: To remove the foundation or support of by clandestine means; to ruin in an underhand way;
unballasted: 1. Etym: [Properly p. p. unballast.] Freed from ballast; having discharged ballast. 2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + ballasted.] Not furnished with ballast; not kept steady by ballast; unsteady; as, unballasted vessels; unballasted wits. Unballasted by any sufficient weight of plan. De Quincey.
unlodge: To dislodge; to deprive of lodgment. Carew.
unisonal: Being in unison; unisonant. -- U*nis"o*nal*ly, adv.
unicursal: That can be passed over in a single course; -- said of a curve when the coördinates of the point on the curve can be expressed as rational algebraic functions of a single parameter th.
unsorted: 1. Not sorted; not classified; as, a lot of unsorted goods. 2. Not well selected; ill-chosen. The purpose you undertake is dangerous; the friends you named uncertain; the time itself unsorted. Shak.
uniparous: 1. (Zoöl.) Producing but one egg or young at a time. 2. (Bot.) Producing but one axis of inflorescence; -- said of the scorpioid cyme.
unsatiable: Insatiable. (old) Hooker. -- Un*sa"ti*a*ble*ness, n. (old) -- Un*sa"ti*a*bly, adv. (old)
uncleship: The office or position of an uncle. Lamb.
unwist: 1. Not known; unknown. (old) Chaucer. Spenser. 2. Not knowing; unwitting. (old) Wyclif.
unkind: Having no race or kindred; childless. [Obs. & R.] Shak. | 1. Not kind; contrary to nature, or the law of kind or kindred; unnatural. (old) "Such unkind abominations." Chaucer. 2. Wanting in kindness, sympathy, benevolence, gratitude, or the like; cruel;
unlike: 1. Not like; dissimilar; diverse; having no resemblance; as, the cases are unlike. 2. Not likely; improbable; unlikely. [Obsoles.] Unlike quantities (Math.), quantities expressed by letters which are different or of different powers, as a, b, c, a2, a3, xn, and the like. -- Unlike signs (Math.), the signs plus (+) and minus (-).
ungka: The siamang; -- called also ungka ape.
unicolorous: Having the surface of a uniform color.
uncoif: To deprive of the coif or cap. Young.
undermasted: Having masts smaller than the usual dimension; -- said of vessels. Totten.
unturned: Not turned; not revolved or reversed. To leave no stone unturned, to leave nothing untried for accomplishing one's purpose. [He] left unturned no stone To make my guilt appear, and hide his own. Dryden.
undercrest: To support as a crest; to bear. [Obs. & R.] Shak.
unabsorbable: Not absorbable; specifically (Physiol.), not capable of absorption; unable to pass by osmosis into the circulating blood; as, the unabsorbable portion of food.
unconcerning: Not interesting of affecting; insignificant; not belonging to one. (old) Addison.
unsincerity: The quality or state of being unsincere or impure; insincerity. (old) Boyle.
underhanded: 1. Underhand; clandestine. 2. Insufficiently provided with hands or workers; short-handed; sparsely populated. Norway . . . might defy the world, . . . but it is much underhanded now. Coleridge.
undreamed: Not dreamed, or dreamed of; not thof. Unpathed waters, undreamed shores. Shak.
ungain: Ungainly; clumsy; awkward; also, troublesome; inconvenient. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Beau. & Pl.
unman: 1. To deprive of the distinctive qualities of a human being, as reason, or the like. South. 2. To emasculate; to deprive of virility. 3. To deprive of the courage and fortitude of a man; to break or subdue the manly spirit in; to cause to despond; to dishearten; to make womanish. Let's not unman each other. Byron. 4. To deprive of men; as, to unman a ship.
unifollilate: Having only one leaflet, as the leaves of the orange tree.
unchristian: 1. Not Christian; not converted to the Christian faith; infidel. 2. Contrary to Christianity; not like or becoming a Christian; as, unchristian conduct. | To make unchristian. (old) South.
unsacrament: To deprive of sacramental character or efficacy; as, to unsacrament the rite of baptism. (old)
unadulterated: Not adulterated; pure. "Unadulterate air." Cowper. -- Un`a*dul"ter*ate*ly, adv.
underwitted: Weak in intellect; half-witted; silly. Bp. Kennet.
unmarry: To annul the marriage of; to divorce. Milton.
unaccomplished: Not accomplished or performed; unfinished; also, deficient in accomplishment; unrefined.
undergraduate: A member of a university or a college who has not taken his first degree; a student in any school who has not completed his course. | Of or pertaining to an undergraduate, or the body of undergraduates.
unharness: 1. To strip of harness; to loose from harness or gear; as, to unharness horses or oxen. Cowper. 2. To disarm; to divest of armor. Holinshed.
unpreach: To undo or overthrow by preaching. De Foe.
unfolder: One who, or that which, unfolds.
undervaluation: The act of undervaluing; a rate or value not equal to the real worth.
unalienable: Inalienable; as, unalienable rights. Swift. -- Un*al"ien*a*bly, adv.
unspilt: Not spilt or wasted; not shed.
unappropriated: 1. Not specially appropriate; having not special application. J. Warton. 2. Not granted to any person, corporation, or the like, to the exclusion of others; as, unappropriated lands. 3. Not granted for, or applied to, any specific purpose; as, the unappropriated moneys in the treasury.
unfool: To restore from folly, or from being a fool. (old) Shak.
unio: Any one of numerous species of fresh-water mussels belonging to Unio and many allied genera.
unsparing: 1. Not sparing; not parsimonious; liberal; profuse. Burke. 2. Not merciful or forgiving. Milton. -- Un*spar"ing*ly, adv. -- Un*spar"ing*ness, n.
unfounded: 1. Not founded; not built or established. Milton. 2. Having no foundation; baseless; vain; idle; as, unfounded expectations. Paley.
unparadise: To deprive of happiness like that of paradise; to render unhappy. Young.
unruliment: Unruliness. (old) "Breaking forth with rude unruliment." Spenser.
unglue: To separate, part, or open, as anything fastened with glue. She stretches, gapes, unglues her eyes, And asks if it be time to rise. Swift.
unhitch: To free from being hitched, or as if from being hitched; to unfasten; to loose; as, to unhitch a horse, or a trace.
unintermission: Want or failure of intermission. Bp. Parker.
unkennel: 1. To drive from a kennel or hole; as, to unkennel a fox. 2. Fig.: To discover; to disclose. Shak.
unijugate: Having but one pair of leaflets; -- said of a pinnate leaf.
unbreast: To disclose, or lay open; to unbosom. (old) P. Fletcher,
unhouse: To drive from a house or habitation; to dislodge; hence, to deprive of shelter.
undulated: 1. Resembling, or in the nature of, waves; having a wavy surface; undulatory. 2. (Bot.) Waved obtusely up and down, near the margin, as a leaf or corolla; wavy. 3. (Zoöl.) Formed with elevations and depressions resembling waves; having wavelike color markings; as, an undulated shell.
unbox: To remove from a box or boxes.
unarted: 1. Ignorant of the arts. (old) E. Waterhouse. 2. Not artificial; plain; simple. (old) Feltham.
unequalness: The quality or state of being unequal; inequality; unevenness. Jer. Taylor.
unpleat: To remove the plaits of; to smooth. W. Browne.
unmanhood: Absence or lack of manhood. (old) Chaucer.
unappropriate: 1. Inappropriate; unsuitable. 2. Not appropriated. Bp. Warburton. | To take from private possession; to restore to the possession or right of all; as, to unappropriate a monopoly. Milton.
unprotestantize: To render other than Protestant; to cause to change from Protestantism to some other form of religion; to deprive of some Protestant feature or characteristic. The attempt to unprotestantize the Church of England. Froude.
undersecretary: A secretary who is subordinate to the chief secretary; an assistant secretary; as, an undersecretary of the Treasury.
unkent: Unknown; strange. [Obs. or Scot.] W. Browne.
unravelment: The act of unraveling, or the state of being unraveled.
unrevenued: Not furnished with a revenue. Milton.
unpinion: To loose from pinions or manacles; to free from restraint. Goldsmith.
unfit: To make unsuitable or incompetent; to deprive of the strength, skill, or proper qualities for anything; to disable; to incapacitate; to disqualify; as, sickness unfits a man for labor; | Not fit; unsuitable. -- Un*fit"ly, adv. -- Un*fit"ness, n.
unplight: To unfold; to lay open; to explain. (old) Chaucer.
unscrupulous: Not scrupulous; unprincipled. -- Un*scru"pu*lous*ly, adv. -- Un*scru"pu*lous*ness, n.
undeify: To degrade from the state of deity; to deprive of the character or qualities of a god; to deprive of the reverence due to a god. Addison.
unwrite: To cancel, as what is written; to erase. Milton.
uncouth: 1. Unknown. (old) "This uncouth errand." Milton. To leave the good that I had in hand, In hope of better that was uncouth. Spenser. 2. Uncommon; rare; exquisite; elegant. (old) Harness . . . so uncouth and so rish. Chaucer. 3. Unfamiliar; strange; hence, mysterious; dreadful; also, odd; awkward; boorish; as, uncouth manners. "Uncouth in guise and gesture." I. Taylor.
unyoked: 1. Not yet yoked; not having worn the yoke. 2. Freed or loosed from a yoke. 3. Licentious; unrestrained. Shak.
unforgettable: Not forgettable; enduring in memory. Pungent and unforgettable truths. Emerson.
unawares: , Without design or preparation; suddenly; without premeditation, unexpectedly. "Mercies lighting unawares." J. H. Newman. Lest unawares we lose This our high place, our sanctuary, our hill. Milton. At unaware, or At unawares, unexpectedly; by surprise. He breaks at unawares upon our walks. Dryden. So we met In this old sleepy town an at unaware. R. Browning.
unciform: Having the shape of a hook; being of a curved or hooked from; hooklike. Unciform bone (Anat.), a bone of the carpus at the bases of the fourth and fifth metacarpals; the hamatum. | The unciform bone. See Illust. of Perissodactyla.
unworship: To deprive of worship or due honor; to dishonor. (old) Wyclif. | Lack of worship or respect; dishonor. (old) Gower.
unkempt: 1. Not combed; disheveled; as, an urchin with unkempt hair. 2. Fig.; Not smoothed; unpolished; rough. My rhymes be rugged and unkempt. Spenser.
underpeep: To peep under. "The flame . . . would underpeep her lids." Shak.
undersign: To write one's name at the foot or end of, as a letter or any legal instrument. The undersigned, the person whose name is signed, or the persons whose names are signed, at the end of a document; the subscriber or subscribers.
underhangman: An assistant or deputy hangman. Shak.
unsay: To recant or recall, as what has been said; to refract; to take back again; to make as if not said. You can say and unsay things at pleasure. Goldsmith.
underlying: Lying under or beneath; hence, fundamental; as, the underlying strata of a locality; underlying principles.
unfertile: Not fertile; infertile; barren. -- Un*fer"tile*ness, n.
unde: Waving or wavy; -- applied to ordinaries, or division lines.
ungracious: 1. Not gracious; showing no grace or kindness; being without good will; unfeeling. Shak. 2. Having no grace; graceless; wicked. (old) Shak. 3. Not well received; offensive; unpleasing; unacceptable; not favored. Anything of grace toward the Irish rebels was as ungracious at Oxford as at London. Clarendon. -- Un*gra"cious*ly, adv. -- Un*gra"cious*ness, n.
unsceptered: 1. Etym: [Pref. un- not + sceptered.] Having no scepter. 2. Etym: [1st pref. un- + scepter.] Deprived of a scepter.
unto: 1. To; -- now used only in antiquated, formal, or scriptural style. See To. 2. Until; till. (old) "He shall abide it unto the death of the priest." Num. xxxv. 25. | Until; till. (old) "Unto this year be gone." Chaucer.
unimpeachable: Not impeachable; not to be called in question; exempt from liability to accusation; free from stain, guilt, or fault; irreproachable; blameless; as, an unimpeachable reputation; unimpeachable testimony. Burke. -- Un`im*peach"a*ble*ness, n. -- Un`im*peach"a*bly, adv.
unguinous: Consisting of, or resembling, fat or oil; oily; unctuous; oleaginous.
underthing: Something that is inferior and of little worth. (old) Beau. & Fl.
unethes: With difficulty; scarcely. See Uneath. [Written also unethe, unneth, unnethe, unnethes, etc.] (old) Chaucer.
unsad: Unsteady; fickle. (old) O, stormy people, unsad and ever untrue. Chaucer.
underjoin: To join below or beneath; to subjoin. Wyclif.
unbeat: To deliver from the form or nature of a beast.
unrealize: To make unreal; to idealize. His fancy . . . unrealizes everything at a touch. Lowell.
unstrained: 1. Not strained; not cleared or purified by straining; as, unstrained oil or milk. 2. Not forced; easy; natural; as, a unstrained deduction or inference. Hakewill.
uncombine: To separate, as substances in combination; to release from combination or union. Daniel.
untruthful: Not truthful; unveracious; contrary to the truth or the fact. -- Un*truth"ful*ly, adv. -- Un*truth"ful*ness, n.
unboundably: Infinitely. (old) I am . . . unboundably beholding to you. J. Webster (1607).
unpursed: 1. Robbed of a purse, or of money. Pollock. 2. Taken from the purse; expended. (old) Gower.
unnest: To eject from a nest; to unnestle. T. Adams.
unshell: To strip the shell from; to take out of the shell; to hatch.
uncork: To draw the cork from; as, to uncork a bottle.
unearthly: Not terrestrial; supernatural; preternatural; hence, weird; appalling; terrific; as, an unearthly sight or sound. -- Un*earth"li*ness, n.
underfurnish: To supply with less than enough; to furnish insufficiently. Collier.
undercurrent: 1. A current below the surface of water, sometimes flowing in a contrary direction to that on the surface. Totten. 2. Hence, figuratively, a tendency of feeling, opinion, or the like, in a direction… | Running beneath the surface; hidden. "Undercurrent woe." Tennyson.
unhoused: 1. Etym: [Properly p. p. of unhouse.] Driven from a house; deprived of shelter. 2. Etym: [Pref. un- + housed.] Not provided with a house or shelter; houseless; homeless.
undispensable: 1. Indispensable. 2. Unavoidable; inevitable. (old) Fuller. 3. Not to be freed by dispensation. (old)
unship: 1. To take out of a ship or vessel; as, to unship goods. 2. (Naut.) To remove or detach, as any part or implement, from its proper position or connection when in use; as, to unship an oar; to unship capstan bars; to unship the tiller.
unruly: Not submissive to rule; disregarding restraint; disposed to violate; turbulent; ungovernable; refractory; as, an unruly boy; unruly boy; unruly conduct. But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison. James iii. 8.
univocacy: The quality or state of being univocal. Sir T. Browne.
unbowel: To deprive of the entrails; to disembowel. Dr. H. More.
unpredict: To retract or falsify a previous prediction. Milton.
underfringe: A lower fringe; a fringe underneath something. Broad-faced, with underfringe of russet beard. Tennyson.
undercraft: A sly trick or device; as, an undercraft of authors. Sterne.
unsymmetrical: 1. Wanting in symmetry, or due proportion pf parts. 2. (Biol.) Not symmetrical; being without symmetry, as the parts of a flower when similar parts are of different size and shape, or when the parts of successive circles differ in number. See Symmetry. 3. (Chem.) Being without symmetry of chemical structure or relation; as, an unsymmetrical carbon atom.
unbody: To free from the body; to disembody. Her soul unbodied of the burdenous corse. Spenser. | To leave the body; to be disembodied; -- said of the soul or spirit. Chaucer.
undraw: To draw aside or open; to draw back. Angels undrew the curtain of the throne. Young.
unspell: To break the power of (a spell); to release (a person) from the influence of a spell; to disenchant. Such practices as these, . . . The more judicious Israelites unspelled. Dryden.
unconsiderate: Inconsiderate; heedless; careless. (old) Daniel. -- Un`con*sid"er*ate*ness, n. (old) Hales.
unequivocal: Not equivocal; not doubtful; not ambiguous; evident; sincere; plain; as, unequivocal evidence; unequivocal words. -- Un`e*quiv"o*cal*ly, adv. -- Un`e*quiv"o*cal*ness, n.
ungainliness: The state or quality of being ungainly; awkwardness.
unparalleled: Having no parallel, or equal; unequaled; unmatched. The unparalleled perseverance of the armies of the United States, under every suffering and discouragement, was little short of a miracle. Washington.
uncompromising: Not admitting of compromise; making no truce or concessions; obstinate; unyielding; inflexible. -- Un*com"pro*mi`sing*ly, adv.
unitable: Capable of union by growth or otherwise. Owen.
unreprievable: Not capable of being reprieved. Shak.
unlace: 1. To loose by undoing a lacing; as, to unlace a shoe. 2. To loose the dress of; to undress; hence, to expose; to disgrace. What's the matter, That you unlace your reputation thus Shak. 3. (Naut.) To loose, and take off, as a bonnet from a sail, or to cast off, as any lacing in any part of the rigging of a vessel. Totten.
underneath: Beneath; below; in a lower place; under; as, a channel underneath the soil. Or sullen mole, that runneth underneath. Milton. | Under; beneath; below. Underneath this stone lie As much beauty as could die. B. Jonson.
undeceive: To cause to be no longer deceived; to free from deception, fraud, fallacy, or mistake. South.
unprayed: Not prayed for. (old) Sir T. More.
uncared: Not cared for; not heeded; -- with for.
unnerve: To deprive of nerve, force, or strength; to weaken; to enfeeble; as, to unnerve the arm. Unequal match'd, . . . The unnerved father falls. Shak.
unifilar: Having only one thread; involving the use of only one thread, wire, fiber, or the like; as, unifilar suspension. Unifilar magnetometer (Physics), an instrument which consists of a magnetic bar suspended at its center of gravity by a long thread, constituting a delicate means for accurately measuring magnetic intensities, also for determining declinations of the magnetic needle.
unremitting: Not remitting; incessant; continued; persevering; as, unremitting exertions. Cowper. -- Un`re*mit"ting*ly, adv. -- Un`re*mit"ting*ness, n.
unsighted: 1. Not sighted, or seen. Suckling. 2. (Gun.) Not aimed by means of a sight; also, not furnished with a sight, or with a properly adjusted sight; as, to shoot and unsighted rife or cannon.
univariant: Having one degree of freedom or variability.
unwell: 1. Not well; indisposed; not in good health; somewhat ill; ailing. 2. (Med.) Specifically, ill from menstruation; affected with, or having, catamenial; menstruant. Note: This word was formerly regarded as an Americanism, but is now in common use among all who speak the English language.
untwain: To rend in twain; to tear in two. (old) Skelton.
uneven: 1. Not even; not level; not uniform; rough; as, an uneven road or way; uneven ground. 2. Not equal; not of equal length. Hebrew verse consists of uneven feet. Peacham. 3. Not divisible by two without a remainder; odd; -- said of numbers; as, 3, 7, and 11 are uneven numbers. Un*e"ven*ly, adv. -- Un*e"ven*ness, n.
universologist: One who is versed in universology.
unity: 1. The state of being one; oneness. Whatever we can consider as one thing suggests to the understanding the idea of unity. Locks. Note: Unity is affirmed of a simple substance or indivisible monad, or of several particles or parts so intimately and closely united as to constitute a separate body or thing. See the Synonyms under Union. 2. Concord; harmony; conjunction;
unsaturated: 1. Capable of absorbing or dissolving to a greater degree; as, an unsaturated solution. 2. (Chem.) Capable of taking up, or of uniting with, certain other elements or compounds, without the elimination of any side product; thus, aldehyde, ethylene, and ammonia are unsaturated.
uncovenanted: 1. Not covenanted; not granted or entered into under a covenant, agreement, or contract. Bp. Horsley. 2. Not having joined in a league, or assented to a covenant or agreement, as to the Solemn League and Covenant of the Scottish people in the times of the Stuarts. In Scotland a few fanatical nonjurors may have grudged their allegiance to an uncovenanted king. Sir T. E. May. 3.
underestimate: The act of underestimating; too low an estimate.
unsocket: To loose or take from a socket.
undifferentiated: Not differentiated; specifically (Biol.), homogenous, or nearly so; -- said especially of young or embryonic tissues which have not yet undergone differentiation (see Differentiation, 3), that is, which show no visible separation into their different structural parts.
unicostate: Having a single rib or strong nerve running upward from the base; -- said of a leaf.
unjust: 1. Acting contrary to the standard of right; not animated or controlled by justice; false; dishonest; as, an unjust man or judge. 2. Contrary to justice and right; prompted by a spirit of injustice; wrongful; as, an unjust sentence; an unjust demand; an unjust accusation. -- Un*just"ly, adv. -- Un*just"ness, n.
undercut: The lower or under side of a sirloin of beef; the fillet. | To cut away, as the side of an object, so as to leave an overhanging portion.
undecolic: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid, C11H18O2, of the propiolic acid series, obtained indirectly from undecylenic acid as a white crystalline substance.
underhang: To hang under or down; to suspend. Holland.
unarm: To puff off, or lay down, one's arms or armor. "I'll unarm again." Shak.
unhoped: Not hoped or expected. "With unhoped success." Dryden. Blessings of friends, which to my door Unasked, unhoped, have come. J. N. Newman.
unsupportable: Insupportable; unendurable. -- Un`sup*port"a*ble*ness, n. Bp. Wilkins. -- Un`sup*port"a*bly, adv.
unruled: 1. Not governed or controlled. "Unruled and undirected." Spenser. 2. Not ruled or marked with lines; as, unruled paper.
unbit: To remove the turns of (a rope or cable) from the bits; as, to unbit a cable. Totten.
underplot: 1. A series of events in a play, proceeding collaterally with the main story, and subservient to it. Dryden. 2. A clandestine scheme; a trick. Addison.
unweeting: Unwitting. (old) Chaucer. Spenser. -- Un*weet"ing*ly, adv. (old) Milton.
unconditional: Not conditional limited, or conditioned; made without condition; absolute; unreserved; as, an unconditional surrender. O, pass not, Lord, an absolute decree, Or bind thy sentence unconditional. Dryden. -- Un`con*di"tion*al*ly, adv.
underboard: Under the board, or table; hence, secretly; unfairly; underhand. See the Note under Aboveboard.
unlawful: Not lawful; contrary to law. -- Un*law"ful*ly, adv. -- Un*law"ful*ness, n. Unlawful assembly. (Law) See under Assembly.
unspeakable: Not speakable; incapable of being uttered or adequately described; inexpressible; unutterable; ineffable; as, unspeakable grief or rage. -- Un*speak"a*bly, adv. Ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory. 1 Pet. i. 8.
undersky: The lower region of the sky. Floating about the undersky. Tennyson.
unbreathed: 1. Not breathed. 2. Not exercised; unpracticed. (old) "Their unbreathed memories." Shak.
unbred: 1. Not begotten; unborn. (old) "Thou age unbred." Shak. 2. Not taught or trained; -- with to. Dryden. 3. Not well-bred; ill-bred. (old) Locke.
unceasable: Not capable of being ended; unceasing.
unbeseem: To be unbecoming or unsuitable to; to misbecome.
unique: Being without a like or equal; unmatched; unequaled; unparalleled; single in kind or excellence; sole. -- U*nique"ly, adv. -- U*nique"ness, n. | A thing without a like; something unequaled or unparalleled. The phenix, the unique pf birds. De Quincey.
unright: Not right; wrong. (old) Gower. | A wrong. (old) Nor did I you never unright. Chaucer.
ungodly: 1. Not godly; not having regard for God; disobedient to God; wicked; impious; sinful. 2. Polluted by sin or wickedness. The hours of this ungodly day. Shak. -- Un*god"li*ly, adv. -- Un*god"li*ness, n.
unconning: Not knowing; ignorant. (old) Chaucer. -- n. Ignorance. (old)
unclasp: To loose the clasp of; to open, as something that is fastened, or as with, a clasp; as, to unclasp a book; to unclasp one's heart.
unmuzzle: To loose from a muzzle; to remove a muzzle from.
underminister: To serve, or minister to, in a subordinate relation. (old) Wyclif.
univalence: The quality or state of being univalent.
undermirth: Suppressed or concealed mirth. (old) The Coronation.
unflesh: To deprive of flesh; to reduce a skeleton. "Unfleshed humanity." Wordsworth.
unburden: 1. To relieve from a burden. 2. To throw off, as a burden; to unload.
uncomely: Not comely. -- adv. In an uncomely manner. 1 Cor. vii. 36.
unacceptable: Not acceptable; not pleasing; not welcome; unpleasant; disagreeable; displeasing; offensive. -- Un`ac*cept"a*ble*ness, n. -- Un`ac*cept"a*bly, adv.
underplant: To plant under; specif. (Forestry), to plant (young trees) under an existing stand.
uncertain: 1. Not certain; not having certain knowledge; not assured in mind; distrustful. Chaucer. Man, without the protection of a superior Being, . . . is uncertain of everything that he hopes for. | To make uncertain. (old) Sir W. Raleigh.
unbed: To raise or rouse from bed. Eels unbed themselves and stir at the noise of thunder. Wa
unlook: To recall or retract, as a look. Richardson.
undern: The time between; the time between sunrise and noon; specifically, the third hour of the day, or nine o'clock in the morning, according to ancient reckoning; hence, mealtime, because formerly the principal meal was eaten at that hour; also, later, the afternoon; the time between dinner and supper. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Betwixt undern and noon was the field all won. R.
understanding: Knowing; intelligent; skillful; as, he is an understanding man. | 1. The act of one who understands a thing, in any sense of the verb; knowledge; discernment; comprehension; interpretation; explanation. 2. An agreement of opinion or feeling;
unglaze: To strip of glass; to remove the glazing, or glass, from, as a window.
unsettlement: The act of unsettling, or state of being unsettled; disturbance. J. H. Newman.
unlay: To untwist; as, to unlay a rope.
unlimited: 1. Not limited; having no bounds; boundless; as, an unlimited expanse of ocean. 2. Undefined; indefinite; not bounded by proper exceptions; as, unlimited terms. "Nothing doth more prevail than unlimited generalities." Hooker. 3. Unconfined; not restrained; unrestricted. Ascribe not unto God such an unlimited exercise of mercy as may destroy his justice. Rogers.
unpastor: To cause to be no longer pastor; to deprive of pastorship. Fuller.
unpraise: To withhold praise from; to deprive of praise.
uniate: A member of the Greek Church, who nevertheless acknowledges the supremacy of the Pope of Rome; one of the United Greeks. Also used adjectively.
unpervert: To free from perversion; to deliver from being perverted; to reconvert. (old)
university: 1. The universe; the whole. (old) Dr. H. More. 2. An association, society, guild, or corporation, esp. one capable of having and acquiring property. (old) The universities, or corporate bodies, at Rome were very numerous. There were corporations of bakers, farmers of the revenue, scribes, and others. Eng. Cyc. 3.
undermeal: 1. The inferior, or after, part of the day; the afternoon. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] In undermeals and in mornings. Chaucer. 2. Hence, something occurring or done in the afternoon; esp., an afternoon meal; supper; also, an afternoon nap; a siesta. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Another great supper, or undermeal, was made ready for them, coming home from ditching and plowing. Withals (1608).
universalistic: Of or pertaining to the whole; universal.
unbonnet: To take a bonnet from; to take off one's bonnet; to uncover; as, to unbonnet one's head. Sir W. Scott.
uncastle: To take a castle from; to turn out of a castle.
unworthy: Not worthy; wanting merit, value, or fitness; undeserving; worthless; unbecoming; -- often with of. -- Un*wor"thi*ly, adv. -- Un*wor"thi*ness, n.
unmeant: Not meant or intended; unintentional. Dryden.
unbusied: Not required to work; unemployed; not busy. These unbusied persons can continue in this playing idleness till it become a toil. Bp. Rainbow
unface: To remove the face or cover from; to unmask; to expose.
unexceptive: Not exceptive; not including, admitting, or being, an exception.
unpractical: Not practical; impractical. "Unpractical questions." H. James. I like him none the less for being unpractical. Lowell.
unsecret: To disclose; to divulge. (old) Bacon. | Not secret; not close; not trusty; indiscreet. (old) "We are unsecret to ourselves." Shak.
unicameral: Having, or consisting of, a single chamber; -- said of a legislative assembly. F. Lieber.
understatement: The act of understating, or the condition of being understated; that which is understated; a statement below the truth.
uncomfortable: 1. Feeling discomfort; uneasy; as, to be uncomfortable on account of one's position. 2. Causing discomfort; disagreeable; unpleasant; as, an uncomfortable seat or situation. The most dead, uncomfortable time of the year. Addison. -- Un*com"fort*a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*com"fort*a*bly, adv.
unfledged: Not fledged; not feathered; hence, not fully developed; immature. Dryden.
uncrudded: Not cruddled, or curdled. (old) Her breast like to a bowl of cream uncrudded. Spenser.
uniterable: Not iterable; incapable of being repeated. (old) "To play away an uniterable life." Sir T. Browne.
unfriend: One not a friend; an enemy. Carlyle.
underwork: 1. To injure by working secretly; to destroy or overthrow by clandestine measure; to undermine. But thou from loving England art so far, That thou hast underwrought his lawful king. Shak. 2. | 1. To work or operate in secret or clandestinely. B. Jonson. 2. To do less work than is proper or suitable. 3. To do work for a less price than current rates.
unpardonable: Not admitting of pardon or forgiveness; inexcusable.
untented: Having no tent or tents, as a soldier or a field. | Not tended; not dressed. See 4th Tent. The untented woundings of a father's curse Pierce every sense about thee! Shak.
uncoined: 1. Not coined, or minted; as, uncoined silver. Locke. 2. Not fabricated; not artificial or counterfeit; natural. "Plain and uncoined constancy." Shak.
underplay: 1. To play in a subordinate, or in an inferior manner; to underact a part. 2. (Card Playing) To play a low card when holding a high one, in the hope of a future advantage.
uncinata: A division of marine chætopod annelids which are furnished with uncini, as the serpulas and sabellas.
underpart: A subordinate part. It should be lightened with underparts of mirth. Dryden.
uncutvelvet: A fabric woven like velvet, but with the loops of the warp threads uncut.
undumpish: To relieve from the dumps. (old) Fuller.
unbear: To remove or loose the bearing rein of (a horse).
unlaugh: To recall, as former laughter. [Obs. & R.] Sir T. More.
unfaith: Absence or want of faith; faithlessness; distrust; unbelief. Faith and unfaith can ne'er be equal powers: Unfaith in aught is want of faith in all. Tennyson.
unstrain: To relieve from a strain; to relax. B. Jonson.
unanswerable: Not answerable; irrefutable; conclusive; decisive; as, he have an unanswerable argument. -- Un*an"swer*a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*an"swer*a*bly, adv.
unweary: To cause to cease being weary; to refresh. (old) Dryden.
unsanctification: Absence or lack of sanctification. Shak.
unresistance: Nonresistance; passive submission; irresistance. Bp. Hall.
ungot: 1. Not gotten; not acquired. 2. Not begotten. [Obs. or Poetic] "His loins yet full of ungot princes." Waller.
undepartable: Incapable of being parted; inseparable. (old) Chaucer. Wyclif.
unportuous: Having no ports. (old) "An unportuous coast." Burke.
unfathered: 1. Having no father; fatherless; hence, born contrary to nature. Shak. 2. Having no acknowledged father; hence, illegitimate; spurious; bastard.
unipersonal: 1. Existing as one, and only one, person; as, a unipersonal God. 2. (Gram.) Used in only one person, especially only in the third person, as some verbs; impersonal.
unrivaled: Having no rival; without a competitor; peerless. [Spelt also unrivalled.] Pope.
unmoral: Having no moral perception, quality, or relation; involving no idea of morality; -- distinguished from both moral and immoral. -- Un`mo*ral"i*ty, n.
undersoil: The soil beneath the surface; understratum; subsoil.
unipolar: 1. (Physics) Having, or acting by means of, one pole only. 2. (Anat.) Having but one pole or process; -- applied to those ganglionic nerve cells which have but one radiating process; -- opposed to multipolar. Unipolar induction (Elec.), induction, as in a conducting circuit, by only one pole of a magnet.
untold: 1. Not told; not related; not revealed; as, untold secrets. 2. Not numbered or counted; as, untold money.
underlock: A lock of wool hanging under the belly of a sheep.
unmistakable: Incapable of being mistaken or misunderstood; clear; plain; obvious; evident. -- Un`mis*tak"a*bly, adv.
underaction: Subordinate action; a minor action incidental or subsidiary to the main story; an episode. The least episodes or underactions . . . are parts necessary or convenient to carry on the main design. Dryden.
unknow: 1. To cease to know; to lose the knowledge of. (old) 2. To fail of knowing; to be ignorant of. (old) | Unknown. (old) "French of Paris was to her unknow." Chaucer.
underbranch: 1. A lower branch. 2. A twig or branchlet. (old) Spenser.
unassured: 1. Not assured; not bold or confident. 2. Not to be trusted. (old) Spenser. 3. Not insured against loss; as, unassured goods.
unaccountability: The quality or state of being unaccountable.
uniat: A member of the Greek Church, who nevertheless acknowledges the supremacy of the Pope of Rome; one of the United Greeks. Also used adjectively.
understair: Of or pertaining to the kitchen, or the servants' quarters; hence, subordinate; menial. (old)
unexpectation: Absence of expectation; want of foresight. (old) Bp. Hall.
unliquidated: Not liquidated; not exactly ascertained; not adjusted or settled. Unliquidated damages (Law), penalties or damages not ascertained in money. Burrill.
unlicked: Not licked; hence, not properly formed; ungainly. Cf. To lick into shape, under Lick, v. Shak.
unbark: To deprive of the bark; to decorticate; to strip; as, to unbark a tree. Bacon. | To cause to disembark; to land. (old) Hakluyt.
undecreed: 1. Etym: [Pref. un- not + decreed.] Not decreed. 2. Etym: [1st pref. un- + decree.] Reversed or nullified by decree, as something previously decreed.
unfeigned: Not feigned; not counterfeit; not hypocritical; real; sincere; genuine; as, unfeigned piety; unfeigned love to man. "Good faith unfeigned." Chaucer. -- Un*feign"ed*ly, adv. -- Un*feign"ed*ness, n.
undertide: The under or after part of the day; undermeal; evening. (old) He, coming home at undertime, there found The fairest creature that he ever saw. Spenser.
uncustomable: Not customable, or subject to custom duties.
undecylenic: Pertaining to, or designating, an acid C11H20O2, homologous with acrylic acid, and obtained as a white crystalline substance by the distillation of castor oil.
unsaddle: 1. To strip of a saddle; to take the saddle from, as a horse. 2. To throw from the saddle; to unhorse.
unswaddle: To take a swaddle from; to unswathe.
unbind: To remove a band from; to set free from shackles or fastenings; to unite; to unfasten; to loose; as, unbind your fillets; to unbind a prisoner's arms; to unbind a load.
unseemliness: The quality or state of being unseemly; unbecomingness. Udall.
unveracity: Want of veracity; untruthfulness; as, unveracity of heart. Carlyle.
undistinctive: Making no distinctions; not discriminating; impartial. As undistinctive Death will come here one day. Dickens.
unexpressive: 1. Not expressive; not having the power of utterance; inexpressive. 2. Incapable of being expressed; inexpressible; unutterable; ineffable. (old) Run, run, Orlando; carve on every tree The fair, the chaste and unexpressive she. Shak. -- Un`ex*press"ive*ly, adv.
unbury: To disinter; to exhume; fig., to disclose.
unconfound: To free from a state of confusion, or of being confounded. Milton.
unrig: To strip of rigging; as, to unrig a ship. Totten.
unifacial: Having but one front surface; as, some foliaceous corals are unifacial, the polyp mouths being confined to one surface.
untressed: Not tied up in tresses; unarranged; -- said of the hair. Chaucer.
unbegilt: Not gilded; hence, not rewarded with gold.
unbelief: 1. The withholding of belief; doubt; incredulity; skepticism. 2. Disbelief; especially, disbelief of divine revelation, or in a divine providence or scheme of redemption. Blind unbelief is sure to err, And scan his work in vain. Cowper. Syn. -- See Disbelief.
unsalable: Not salable; unmerchantable. -- n. That which can not be sold. Byron.
unmitre: To deprive of a miter; to depose or degrade from the rank of a bishop. Milton.
underditch: To dig an underground ditches in, so as to drain the surface; to underdrain; as, to underditch a field or a farm.
unyolden: Not yielded. (old) "[By] force . . . is he taken unyolden." Sir T. Browne.
unthriftiness: The quality or state or being unthrifty; profuseness; lavishness. Udall.
unfortunate: Not fortunate; unsuccessful; not prosperous; unlucky; attended with misfortune; unhappy; as, an unfortunate adventure; an unfortunate man; an unfortunate commander; unfortunate business. -- n. An unfortunate person. Hood. -- Un*for"tu*nate*ly, adv. -- Un*for"tu*nate*ness, n.
unwrinkle: To reduce from a wrinkled state; to smooth.
unwritten: 1. Not written; not reduced to writing; oral; as, unwritten agreements. 2. Containing no writing; blank; as, unwritten paper. Unwritten doctrines (Theol.), such doctrines as have been handed down by word of mouth; oral or traditional doctrines. -- Unwritten law. Etym: [Cf. L.
unhallowed: Not consecrated; hence, profane; unholy; impious; wicked. In the cause of truth, no unhallowed violence . . . is either necessary or admissible. E. D. Griffin.
unartful: Lacking art or skill; artless. Congreve. -- Un*art"ful*ly, adv. Swift. Burke.
unappalled: Not appalled; not frightened; dauntless; undaunted. Milton.
unspeak: To retract, as what has been spoken; to recant; to unsay. Shak.
unware: 1. Unaware; not foreseeing; being off one's guard. (old) Chaucer. Fairfax. 2. Happening unexpectedly; unforeseen. (old) The unware woe of harm that cometh behind. Chaucer. -- Un*ware"ly, adv. (old) -- Un*ware"ness, n. (old)
unburiable: Not ready or not proper to be buried. Tennyson.
unthinker: A person who does not think, or does not think wisely.
underconduct: A lower conduit; a subterranean conduit. (old) Sir H. Wotton.
underbred: Not thoroughly bred; ill-bred; as, an underbred fellow. Goldsmith.
uneasy: 1. Not easy; difficult. Things . . . so uneasy to be satisfactorily understood. Boyle. The road will be uneasy to find. Sir W. Scott. 2. Restless; disturbed by pain, anxiety, or the like; disquieted; perturbed. The soul, uneasy and confined from home, Rests and expatiates in a life to come. Pope. 3. Not easy in manner; constrained; stiff; awkward; not graceful;
unprison: To take or deliver from prison.
unsured: Not made sure. (old) Thy now unsured assurance to the crown. Shak.
unfurnish: To strip of furniture; to divest; to strip.
unqueen: To divest of the rank or authority of queen. Shak.
unbarricadoed: Not obstructed by barricades; open; as, unbarricadoed streets. Burke.
unwisdom: Want of wisdom; unwise conduct or action; folly; simplicity; ignorance. Sumptuary laws are among the exploded fallacies which we have outgrown, and we smile at the unwisdom which could except to regulate private habits and manners by statute. J. A. Froude.
unquestioned: 1. Not called in question; not doubted. 2. Not interrogated; having no questions asked; not examined or examined into. Shak. She muttering prayers, as holy rites she meant, Through the divided crowd unquestioned went. Dryden. 3. Indisputable; not to be opposed or impugned. Their unquestioned pleasures must be served. B. Jonson.
uncloud: To free from clouds; to unvail; to clear from obscurity, gloom, sorrow, or the like. Beau. & Fl.
unbundle: To release, as from a bundle; to disclose.
unroost: To drive from the roost. Shak.
uncertainty: 1. The quality or state of being uncertain. 2. That which is uncertain; something unknown. Our shepherd's case is every man's case that quits a moral certainty for an uncertainty. L'Estrange.
unvessel: To cause to be no longer a vessel; to empty. (old) Ford.
unservice: Neglect of duty; idleness; indolence. (old) Massinger.
unrioted: Free from rioting. (old) "A chaste, unrioted house." May (Lucan).
undecagon: A figure having eleven angles and eleven sides.
undeniable: 1. Not deniable; incapable of denial; palpably true; indisputable; obvious; as, undeniable evidence. 2. Unobjectionable; unquestionably excellent; as, a person of undeniable connections. [Colloq.] G. Eliot.
undecennial: Occurring or observed every eleventh year; belonging to, or continuing, a period of eleven years; undecennary; as, an undecennial festival.
undershirt: A shirt worn next the skin, under another shirt; -- called also undervest.
unlash: To loose, as that which is lashed or tied down.
unstriped: 1. Not striped. 2. (Nat. Hist.) Without marks or striations; nonstriated; as, unstriped muscle fibers.
unsadden: To relieve from sadness; to cheer. Whitlock.
univocation: Agreement of name and meaning. (old) Whiston.
unconformable: 1. Not conformable; not agreeable; not conforming. Moral evil is an action unconformable to it [the rule of our duty]. I. Watts. 2. (Geol.) Not conformable; not lying in a parallel position; as, unconformable strata. -- Un`con*form"a*ble*ness, n. -- Un`con*form"a*bly, adv.
underage: Not having arrived at adult age, or at years of discretion; hence, raw; green; immature; boyish; childish. (old) I myself have loved a lady, and pursued her with a great deal of under-age protestation. J. Webster.
undertake: 1. To take upon one's self; to engage in; to enter upon; to take in hand; to begin to perform; to set about; to attempt. To second, or oppose, or undertake The perilous attempt. Milton. 2. | 1. To take upon one's self, or assume, any business, duty, or province. O Lord, I am oppressed; undertake for me. Isa. xxxviii. 14. 2. To venture; to hazard. (old) It is the cowish terror of his…
unspotted: Not spotted; free from spot or stain; especially, free from moral stain; unblemished; immaculate; as, an unspotted reputation. -- Un*spot"ted*ness, n.
unwitting: Not knowing; unconscious; ignorant. -- Un*wit"ting*ly, adv.
unsoldiered: Not equipped like a soldier; unsoldierlike. (old) J. Fletcher.
unportunate: Importunate; troublesome with requests. (old) Golden Boke.
ungular: Of or pertaining to a hoof, claw, or talon; ungual.
unseal: 1. To break or remove the seal of; to open, as what is sealed; as, to unseal a letter. Unable to unseal his lips beyond the width of a quarter of an inch. Sir W. Scott. 2. To disclose, as a secret. (old) The Coronation.
undersphere: 1. A sphere which is smaller than, and in its movements subject to, another; a satellite. 2. An inferior sphere, or field of action.
untent: To bring out of a tent. Shak.
unroofed: 1. Etym: [Properly p. p. of unroof.] Stripped of a roof, or similar covering. Broken carriages, dead horses, unroofed cottages, all indicated the movements. Sir W. Scott. 2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + roofed.] Not yet roofed.
untitled: 1. Not titled; having no title, or appellation of dignity or distinction. Spenser. 2. Being without title or right; not entitled. Shak.
ungainly: 1. Not gainly; not expert or dexterous; clumsy; awkward; uncouth; as, an ungainly strut in walking. His ungainly figure and eccentric manners. Macaulay. 2. Unsuitable; unprofitable. (old) Hammond.
untile: To take the tiles from; to uncover by removing the tiles.
undecennary: Occurring once in every period of eleven years; undecennial. An undecennary account laid before Parliament. E. Stiles.
unanswerability: The quality of being unanswerable; unanswerableness.
unbarrel: To remove or release from a barrel or barrels.
underpropper: One who, or that which, underprops or supports.
unprecedented: Having no precedent or example; not preceded by a like case; not having the authority of prior example; novel; new; unexampled. -- Un*prec"e*dent*ed*ly, adv.
unhive: 1. To drive or remove from a hive. 2. To deprive of habitation or shelter, as a crowd.
unswear: To recant or recall, as an oath; to recall after having sworn; to abjure. J. Fletcher.
underpoise: To weigh, estimate, or rate below desert; to undervalue. Marston.
unguiculated: 1. Furnished with nails, claws, or hooks; clawed. See the Note under Nail, n., 1. 2. (Bot.) Furnished with a claw, or a narrow stalklike base, as the petals of a carnation.
unroot: To tear up by the roots; to eradicate; to uproot. | To be torn up by the roots. Beau. & Fl.
unguent: A lubricant or salve for sores, burns, or the like; an ointment. Cowper. Note: An unguent is stiffer than a liniment, but softer than a cerate.
uncial: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a certain style of letters used in ancient manuscripts, esp. in Greek and Latin manuscripts. The letters are somewhat rounded, and the upstrokes and downstrokes usually have a slight inclination. These letters were used as early as the 1st century b. c., and were seldom used after the 10th century a. d., being superseded by the cursive style.
unidimensional: Having but one dimension. See Dimension.
unoil: To remove the oil from. Dryden.
unlabored: 1. Not produced by labor or toil. "Unlabored harvests." Dryden. 2. Not cultivated; untitled; as, an unlabored field. 3. Not laboriously produced, or not evincing labor; as, an unlabored style or work. Tickell.
uncinus: One of the peculiar minute chitinous hooks found in large numbers in the tori of tubicolous annelids belonging to the Uncinata.
unbegotten: Not begot; not yet generated; also, having never been generated; self-existent; eternal.
until: 1. To; unto; towards; -- used of material objects. Chaucer. Taverners until them told the same. Piers Plowman. He roused himself full blithe, and hastened them until. Spenser. 2. To; up to; till; | As far as; to the place or degree that; especially, up to the time that; till. See Till, conj. In open prospect nothing bounds our eye, Until the earth seems joined unto the sky. Dryden.
undersparred: Having spars smaller than the usual dimension; -- said of vessels.
unestablish: To disestablish. The Parliament demanded of the king to unestablish that prelatical government. Milton.
uncurl: To loose from curls, or ringlets; to straighten out, as anything curled or curly. He sheaths his paw, uncurls his angry mane. Dryden. | To become uncurled, or straight.
unilateral: 1. Being on one side only; affecting but one side; one-sided. 2. (Biol.) Pertaining to one side; one-sided; as, a unilateral raceme, in which the flowers grow only on one side of a common axis, or are all turned to one side. Unilateral contract (Law), a contract or engagement requiring future action only by one party.
unbarbed: 1. Not shaven. (old) 2. Destitute of bards, or of reversed points, hairs, or plumes; as, an unbarded feather.
undecyl: The radical regarded as characteristic of undecylic acid.
underfong: 1. To undertake; to take in hand; to receive. (old) Piers Plowman. Rom. of R. 2. To insnare; to circumvent. (old) Spenser. 3. To sustain; to support; to guard. Nash.
unfeeling: 1. Destitute of feeling; void of sensibility; insensible; insensate. 2. Without kind feelings; cruel; hard-hearted. To each his sufferings: all are men, Condemned alike to groan; The tender for another's pain, Th' unfeeling for his own. Gray. -- Un*feel"ing*ly, adv. -- Un*feel"ing*ness, n.
unculture: Want of culture. "Idleness, ill husbandry . . . unculture." Bp. Hall.
unfailable: Infallible. (old) "This unfailable word of truth." Bp. Hall.
unwoman: To deprive of the qualities of a woman; to unsex. R. Browning.
underwriter: One who underwrites his name to the conditions of an insurance policy, especially of a marine policy; an insurer.
unboy: To divest of the traits of a boy. Clarendon.
unpolled: Not polled. Specifically: (a) Not enumerated or registered; as, an unpolled vote or voter. (b) Not plundered. (old) "Unpoll'd Arabian wealth." Fanshawe.
unorganized: Not organized; being without organic structure; specifically (Biol.), not having the different tissues and organs characteristic of living organisms, nor the power of growth and development; as, the unorganized ferments. See the Note under Ferment, n., 1.
unreality: The quality or state of being unreal; want of reality.
unsecularize: To cause to become not secular; to detach from secular things; to alienate from the world.
unrest: Want of rest or repose; unquietness; sleeplessness; uneasiness; disquietude. Is this, quoth she, the cause of your unrest! Chaucer. Can calm despair and wild unrest Be tenants of a single breast Tennyson.
unvote: To reverse or annul by vote, as a former vote. Bp, Burnet.
unhook: To loose from a hook; to undo or open by loosening or unfastening the hooks of; as, to unhook a fish; to unhook a dress.
unprincipled: Being without principles; especially, being without right moral principles; also, characterized by absence of principle. -- Un*prin"ci*pled*ness, n.
unrivet: To take out, or loose, the rivets of; as, to unrivet boiler plates.
uniserial: Having only one row or series.
unbid: 1. Not bidden; not commanded. Thorns also and thistles it shall bring thee forth Unbid; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field. Milton. 2. Uninvited; as, unbidden guests. Shak. 3. Being without a prayer. (old) Spenser.
unpope: 1. To divest of the character, office, or authority of a pope. 2. To deprive of a pope. (old) Rome will never so far unpope herself as to part with her pretended supremacy. Fuller.
unicarinated: Having one ridge or keel. Craig.
universalist: 1. (Theol.) One who believes in Universalism; one of a denomination of Christians holding this faith. 2. One who affects to understand all the particulars in statements or propositions. (old) Bentley. | Of or pertaining to Unversalists of their doctrines.
unicornous: Having but a single horn; -- said of certain insects. "Unicornous beetles." Sir T. Browne.
underdig: To dig under or beneath; to undermine. (old) Wyclif.
unavoided: 1. Not avoided or shunned. Shak. 2. Unavoidable; inevitable. (old) B. Jonson.
untangle: To loose from tangles or intricacy; to disentangle; to resolve; as, to untangle thread. Untangle but this cruel chain. Prior.
uncentury: To remove from its actual century. It has first to uncentury itself. H. Drummond.
undiscreet: Indiscreet. Chaucer. -- Un`dis*creet"ly, adv. -- -- Un`dis*creet"ness. -- Un`dis*cre"tion, n. Indiscretion.
unexampled: Having no example or similar case; being without precedent; unprecedented; unparalleled. "A revolution . . . unexampled for grandeur of results." De Quincey.
underclay: A stratum of clay lying beneath a coal bed, often containing the roots of coal plants, especially the Stigmaria.
unigeniture: The state of being the only begotten. Bp. Pearson.
undight: To put off; to lay aside, as a garment. (old) Spenser.
unstratified: Not stratified; -- applied to massive rocks, as granite, porphyry, etc., and also to deposits of loose material, as the glacial till, which occur in masses without layers or strata.
undersay: To say by way of derogation or contradiction. (old) Spenser.
unfrock: To deprive or divest or a frock; specifically, to deprive of priestly character or privilege; as, to unfrock a priest.
unhouseled: Not having received the sacrament. (old) [Written also unhouselled.] To die like the houseless dog on yonder common, unshriven and unhouseled. Sir W. Scott.
unslacked: Not slacked; unslaked; as, unslacked lime.
unpeeled: 1. Etym: [1st pref. un- (intensive) + peel.] Thoroughly stripped; pillaged. (old) Shak. 2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + peeled.] Not peeled.
unfaithful: 1. Not faithful; not observant of promises, vows, allegiance, or duty; violating trust or confidence; treacherous; perfidious; as, an unfaithful subject; an unfaithful agent or servant. My feet, through wine, unfaithful to their weight. Pope. His honor rooted in dishonor stood, And faith unfaithful kept him falsely true. Tennyson. 2. Not possessing faith; infidel. Milton.
underheave: To heave or lift from below. (old) Wyclif.
unaccomplishment: The state of being unaccomplished. (old) Milton.
undermatch: One who is not a match for another. Fuller.
unamiability: The quality or state of being unamiable; moroseness.
uncurbable: Not capable of being curbed. Shak.
underconsumption: Consumption of less than is produced; consumption of less than the usual amount. F. A. Walk
underbuilder: A subordinate or assistant builder. An underbuilder in the house of God. Jer. Taylor.
unswayable: Not capable of being swayed. Shak.
unblemished: Not blemished; pure; spotless; as, an unblemished reputation or life. Addison.
unseason: 1. To make unseasoned; to deprive of seasoning. 2. To strike unseasonably; to affect disagreeably or unfavorably. (old) Why do I send this rustic madrigal, That may thy tuneful ear unseason quite Spenser.
unconstant: Not constant; inconstant; fickle; changeable. (old) Shak. -- Un*con"stant*ly, adv. (old) -- Un*con"stant*ness, n. (old)
unwise: Not wise; defective in wisdom; injudicious; indiscreet; foolish; as, an unwise man; unwise kings; unwise measures.
unworldly: Not worldly; spiritual; holy. Hawthorne. -- Un*world"li*ness, n.
unsorrowed: Not sorrowed for; unlamented. Beau. & Fl.
universalian: Of or pertaining to Universalism; Universalist.
uncircumstandtial: 1. Not circumstantial; not entering into minute particulars. 2. Not important; not pertinent; trivial. (old)
unbespeak: To unsay; hence, to annul or cancel. (old) Pepys.
unbishop: To deprive, as a city, of a bishop; to deprive, as a clergyman, of episcopal dignity or rights. "Then he unbishops himself." Milton.
untreasured: 1. Etym: [Properly p. p. of untreasure.] Deprived of treasure. (old) Shak. 2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + treasured.] Not treasured; not kept as treasure.
unison: 1. Harmony; agreement; concord; union. 2. (Mus.) Identity in pitch; coincidence of sounds proceeding from an equality in the number of vibrations made in a given time by two or more sonorous bodies. | 1. Sounding alone. (old) [sounds] intermixed with voice, Choral or unison. Milton. 2. (Mus.) Sounded alike in pitch; unisonant; unisonous; as, unison passages, in which two or more parts unite in…
unfumed: Not exposed to fumes; not fumigated. Milton.
unpen: To release from a pen or from confinement. "If a man unpens another's water." Blackstone.
underministry: A subordinate or inferior ministry. Jer. Taylor.
undeadly: Not subject to death; immortal. (old) -- Un*dead"li*ness, n. (old) Wyclif.
ungown: To strip of a gown; to unfrock.
unsexual: Not sexual; not proper or peculiar to one of the sexes. De Quincey.
unreadiness: The quality or state of being unready.
understate: To state or represent less strongly than may be done truthfully.
undubitable: Indubitable; as, an undubitable principle. (old) Locke.
unhelmet: To deprive of the helmet. Sir W. Scott.
unwind: 1. To wind off; to loose or separate, as what or convolved; to untwist; to untwine; as, to unwind thread; to unwind a ball of yarn. 2. To disentangle. (old) Hooker. | To be or become unwound; to be capable of being unwound or untwisted.
unrude: 1. Not rude; polished. Herrick. 2. Excessively rude. [Obs. & R.] "See how the unrude rascal backbites him." B. Jonson.
unacquaintance: The quality or state of being unacquainted; want of acquaintance; ignorance. He was then in happy unacquaintance with everything connected with that obnoxious cavity. Sir W. Hamilton.
uncomeatable: Not to be come at, or reached; inaccessible. [Colloq.] Addison. My honor is infallible and uncomeatable. Congreve.
unau: The two-toed sloth (Cholopus didactylus), native of South America. It is about two feet long. Its color is a uniform grayish brown, sometimes with a reddish tint.
unhead: 1. To take out the head of; as, to unhead a cask. 2. To decapitate; to behead. (old) T. Brown.
unstudied: 1. Not studied; not acquired by study; unlabored; natural. 2. Not skilled; unversed; -- followed by in. 3. Not spent in study. (old) "To cloak the defects of their unstudied years." Milton.
unconform: Unlike. (old) Not unconform to other shining globes. Milton.
underdrain: An underground drain or trench with openings through which the water may percolate from the soil or ground above. | To drain by forming an underdrain or underdrains in; as, to underdrain land.
unpeered: Having no peer; unequaled; unparalleled. "Unpeered excellence." Marston.
univalent: Having a valence of one; capable of combining with, or of being substituted for, one atom of hydrogen; monovalent; -- said of certain atoms and radicals.
unrobe: To disrobe; to undress; to take off the robes.
underturn: To turn upside down; to subvert; to upset. (old) Wyclif.
undrape: To strip of drapery; to uncover or unveil.
unisilicate: A salt of orthosilicic acid, H4SiO4; -- so called because the ratio of the oxygen atoms united to the basic metals and silicon respectively is 1:1; for example, Mg2SiO4 or 2MgO.SiO2.
unbraid: To separate the strands of; to undo, as a braid; to unravel; to disentangle.
unobservance: Want or neglect of observance; inobservance. Whitlock.
undertaker: 1. One who undertakes; one who engages in any project or business. Beau. & Fl. 2. One who stipulates or covenants to perform any work for another; a contractor. To sign deputations for undertakes to furnish their proportions of saltpeter. Evelyn. In come some other undertakes, and promise us the same or greater wonders. South. 3.
universe: All created things viewed as constituting one system or whole; the whole body of things, or of phenomena; the mundus of the Latins; the world; creation. How may I Adore thee, Author of this universe And all this good to man! Milton.
unprovident: Improvident. (old) "Who for thyself art so unprovident.' Shak.
unchain: To free from chains or slavery; to let loose. Prior.
uncover: 1. To take the cover from; to divest of covering; as, to uncover a box, bed, house, or the like; to uncover one's body. 2. To show openly; to disclose; to reveal. | 1. To take off the hat or cap; to bare the head in token of respect. We are forced to uncover after them. Addison. 2. To remove the covers from dishes, or the like. Uncover, dogs, and lap. Shak.
underwing: 1. (Zoöl.) One of the posterior wings of an insect. 2. (Zoöl.) Any one of numerous species of noctuid moths belonging to Catocala and allied genera, in which the hind wings are banded with red and black or other conspicuous colors. Many of the species are called red underwing.
unprudential: Imprudent. (old) "The most unwise and unprudential act." Milton.
undermaster: A master subordinate to the principal master; an assistant master.
underbear: 1. To support; to endure. (old) Shak. 2. To line; to guard; to face; as, cloth of gold underborne with blue tinsel. (old) Shak.
unhair: To deprive of hair, or of hairs; as, to unhair hides for leather. I 'll unhair thy head. Shak.
unroof: To strip off the roof or covering of, as a house. Shak.
unanchor: To loose from the anchor, as a ship. De Quincey.
underchaps: The lower chaps or jaw. Paley.
unbeing: Not existing. (old) "Beings yet unbeing." Sir T. Browne.
unbacked: 1. Never mounted by a rider; unbroken. "Unbacked colts." Shak. 2. Not supported or encouraged; not countenanced; unaided. Daniel.
unobtrusive: Not obtrusive; not presuming; modest. -- Un`ob*tru"sive*ly, adv. -- Un`ob*tru"sive*ness, n.
uncia: 1. (Rom. Antiq.) A twelfth part, as of the Roman as; an ounce. 2. (Alg.) A numerical coefficient in any particular case of the binomial theorem. (old)
untemper: To deprive of temper, or of the proper degree of temper; to make soft.
unnecessity: The state of being unnecessary; something unnecessary. (old)
uncharm: To release from a charm, fascination, or secret power; to disenchant. Beau. & Fl.
unprinciple: To destroy the moral principles of.
unperfect: To mar or destroy the perfection of. (old) Sir P. Sidney. | Imperfect. (old) Holland. -- Un*per"fect*ly, adv. (old) Hales. -- Un*per"fect*ness, n. (old)
unparched: Dried up; withered by heat. (old) "My tongue . . . unparched." Crashaw.
uncart: To take from, or set free from, a cart; to unload.
undulationist: One who advocates the undulatory theory of light. Whewell.
untrusser: One who untrussed persons for the purpose of flogging them; a public whipper. (old) B. Jonson.
unravel: 1. To disentangle; to disengage or separate the threads of; as, to unravel a stocking. 2. Hence, to clear from complication or difficulty; to unfold; to solve; as, to unravel a plot. 3. | To become unraveled, in any sense.
underrate: To rate too low; to rate below the value; to undervalue. Burke. | A price less than the value; as, to sell a thing at an underrate. Cowley.
underhung: 1. (Carp.) Resting on a track at the bottom, instead of being suspended; - - said of a sliding door. Forney. 2. Having the lower jaw projecting. T. Hughes. | Of an automobile body, suspended from the springs in such a manner that the frame of the chassis is below the axles, the object being to lower the center of gravity of the car.
unbaned: Wanting a band or string; unfastened. (old) Shak.
unthrift: 1. Want of thrift; untriftiness; prodigality. 2. An unthrifty. (old) Dryden.
undated: Rising and falling in waves toward the margin, as a leaf; waved. | Not dated; having no date; of unknown age; as, an undated letter.
unattire: To divest of attire; to undress.
underkeep: To keep under, or in subjection; to suppress. (old) Spenser.
unsquire: To divest of the title or privilege of an esquire. Swift.
undergrove: A grove of shrubs or low trees under taller ones. Wordsworth.
unrein: To loosen the reins of; to remove restraint from. Addison.
undersetter: One who, or that which, undersets or supports; a prop; a support; a pedestal.
unmartyr: To degrade from the rank of a martyr. (old) Fuller.
untomb: To take from the tomb; to exhume; to disinter. Fuller.
uni: A prefix signifying one, once; as in uniaxial, unicellular.
unshroud: To remove the shroud from; to uncover. P. Fletcher.
unsucceedable: Not able or likely to succeed. (old) Sir T. Browne.
unsophisticate: Not sophisticated; pure; innocent; genuine. -- Un`so*phis"ti*ca`ted*ness, n.
uncalledfor: Not called for; not required or needed; improper; gratuitous; wanton.
untimely: Not timely; done or happening at an unnatural, unusual, or improper time; unseasonable; premature; inopportune; as, untimely frosts; untimely remarks; an untimely death. | Out of the natural or usual time; inopportunely; prematurely; unseasonably. "Let them know . . . what's untimely done." Shak.
unmosaic: Not according to Moses; unlike Moses or his works. By this reckoning Moses should be most un Mosaic. Milton.
unswathe: To take a swathe from; to relieve from a bandage; to unswaddle. Addison.
underback: A vessel which receives the wort as it flows from the mashing tub.
unconsidered: Not considered or attended to; not regarded; inconsiderable; trifling. A snapper-up of unconsidered trifles. Shak.
unwitch: To free from a witch or witches; to fee from witchcraft. B. Jonson.
unheart: To cause to lose heart; to dishearten. (old) Shak.
unsaint: To deprive of saintship; to deny sanctity to. South.
uncredit: To cause to be disbelieved; to discredit. (old) Fuller.
unsweat: To relieve from perspiration; to ease or cool after exercise or toil. Milton.
unbosom: To disclose freely; to reveal in confidence, as secrets; to confess; -- often used reflexively; as, to unbosom one's self. Milton.
uneasiness: 1. The quality or state of being uneasy; restlessness; disquietude; anxiety. 2. The quality of making uneasy; discomfort; as, the uneasiness of the road. (old) Bp. Burnet.
unsinew: To deprive of sinews or of strength. Dryden.
unbethink: To change the mind of (one's self). (old)
unequally: In an unequal manner. Unequally pinnate (Bot.), pinnate, but with an odd number of leaflets.
unitive: Having the power of uniting; causing, or tending to produce, union. Jer. Taylor.
unmanned: 1. Etym: [Properly p. p. of unman.] Deprived of manly qualities; deficient in vigor, strength, courage, etc.; weak; effeminate. 2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + man + -ed.] (Falconry) Not tamed; not made familiar with, or subject to, man; -- also used figuratively. (old) Hood my unmanned blood bating in my cheeks With thy black mantle. Shak. 3. Etym: [Pref.
unknowledged: Not acknowledged or recognized. (old) For which bounty to us lent Of him unknowledged or unsent. B. Jonson.
unreproved: 1. Not reproved. Sandys. 2. Not having incurred reproof, blameless. (old) In unreproved pleasures free. Milton.
unargued: 1. Not argued or debated. 2. Not argued against; undisputed. (old) Milton. 3. Not censured. [A Latinism. Obs.] B. Jonson.
unambition: The absence of ambition. F. W. Newman.
undernime: 1. To receive; to perceive. (old) He the savor undernom Which that the roses and the lilies cast. Chaucer. 2. To reprove; to reprehend. (old) Piers Plowman.
unappealable: 1. Not appealable; that can not be carried to a higher tribunal by appeal; as, an unappealable suit or action. 2. Not to be appealed from; -- said of a judge or a judgment that can not be overruled. The infallible, unappealable Judge [God]. South. We submitted to a galling yet unappealable necessity. Shelley. -- Un`ap*peal"a*bly, adv.
unshent: Not shent; not disgraced; blameless. (old) Bp. Hall.
unequalable: Not capable of being equaled or paralleled. (old) Boyle.
uncoil: To unwind or open, as a coil of rope. Derham.
unsolder: To separate or disunite, as what has been soldered; hence, to divide; to sunder. [Formerly written also unsoder.] Tennyson.
unctuosity: Quality or state of being unctuous. Sir T. Browne.
unpay: To undo, take back, or annul, as a payment. Shak.
undoing: 1. The reversal of what has been done. 2. Ruin. "The utter undoing of some." Hooker.
unhusked: 1. Etym: [Pref. un- not + husked.] Not husked; having the husk on. 2. Etym: [1 st pref. un- + husk, n.] Having the husk removed; without husk. Bp. Hall.
unpannel: To take the saddle off; to unsaddle. (old) Jervas.
unchastity: The quality or state of being unchaste; lewdness; incontinence.
unhide: To bring out from concealment; to discover. (old) P. Fletcher.
unshed: 1. Not parted or divided, as the hair. (old) Spenser. 2. Not spilt, or made to flow, as blood or tears. Milton.
undulation: 1. The act of undulating; a waving motion or vibration; as, the undulations of a fluid, of water, or of air; the undulations of sound. 2. A wavy appearance or outline; waviness. Evelyn. 3. (Mus.) (a) The tremulous tone produced by a peculiar pressure of the finger on a string, as of a violin. (b) The pulsation caused by the vibrating together of two tones not quite in unison;
unwashed: Not washed or cleansed; filthy; unclean.
unwieldy: Not easily wielded or carried; unmanageable; bulky; ponderous. "A fat, unwieldy body of fifty-eight years old." Clarendon. -- Un*wield"i*ly, adv. -- Un*wield"i*ness, n.
unlikeness: The quality or state of being unlike; want of resemblance; dissimilarity. Tennyson.
undermost: Lowest, as in place, rank, or condition. Addison.
unpucker: To smooth away the puckers or wrinkles of.
unskill: Want of skill; ignorance; unskillfulness. (old) Sylvester.
unguiferous: Producing, having, or supporting nails or claws.
uncharge: 1. To free from a charge or load; to unload. Wyclif. 2. To free from an accusation; to make no charge against; to acquit. Shak.
unstrength: Want of strength; weakness; feebleness. (old) Wyclif.
unpleasantry: 1. Want of pleasantry. 2. A state of disagreement; a falling out. Thackeray.
uncage: To loose, or release, from, or as from, a cage.
uncomprehensive: 1. Unable to comprehend. Narrow-spirited, uncomprehensive zealots. South. 2. Incomprehensible. (old) Shak.
unnail: To remove the nails from; to unfasten by removing nails.
unshaped: Not shaped; shapeless; misshapen; deformed; ugly.
unpaved: 1. Not paved; not furnished with a pavement. Hakewill. 2. Castrated. (old) "Unpaved eunuch." Shak.
unscale: To divest of scales; to remove scales from. [An eagle] purging and unscaling her long-abused sight at the fountain itself of heavenly radiance. Milton.
unlorded: 1. Etym: [Properly p. p. of unlord.] Deprived of the rank of a lord. 2. Etym: [Pref. un- + lorded.] Not raised to the rank of a lord. Milton.
universityextension: The extension of the advantages of university instruction by means of lectures and classes at various centers.
unemployment: Quality or state of being not employed; -- used esp. in economics, of the condition of various social classes when temporarily thrown out of employment, as those engaged for short periods, those whose trade is decaying, and those least competent.
unseat: 1. To throw from one's seat; to deprive of a seat. Cowper. 2. Specifically, to deprive of the right to sit in a legislative body, as for fraud in election. Macaulay.
uncamp: To break up the camp of; to dislodge from camp. If they could but now uncamp their enemies. Milton.
unicapsular: Having but one capsule to each flower.
uncarnate: Not fleshy; specifically, not made flesh; not incarnate. Sir T. Browne.
union: 1. The act of uniting or joining two or more things into one, or the state of being united or joined; junction; coalition; combination. Note: Union differs from connection, as it implies that the bodies are in contact, without an interconnected by the in 2. Agreement and conjunction of mind, spirit, will, affections, or the like; harmony; concord. 3.
unfrequented: Rarely visited; seldom or never resorted to by human beings; as, an unfrequented place or forest. Addison.
unhold: To cease to hold; to unhand; to release. (old) Otway.
untalked: Not talked; not mentioned; -- often with of. Shak.
undesigning: Having no artful, ulterior, or fraudulent purpose; sincere; artless; simple.
uncircumcision: 1. The absence or want of circumcision. 2. (Script.) People not circumcised; the Gentiles.
unbag: To pour, or take, or let go, out of a bag or bags.
uncessant: Incessant. (old) Dr. H. More. -- Un*ces"sant*ly, adv. (old)
underscore: To draw a mark or line under; to underline. J. Tucker.
undergrown: Of small stature; not grown to a full height or size.
unbarricade: To unbolt; to unbar; to open. You shall not unbarricade the door. J. Webster (1623).
unaneled: Not aneled; not having received extreme unction. Shak.
undulate: To cause to move backward and forward, or up and down, in undulations or waves; to cause to vibrate. Breath vocalized, that is, vibrated and undulated. Holder. | To move in, or have, undulations or waves; to vibrate; to wave; as, undulating air.
unstick: To release, as one thing stuck to another. Richardson.
unpitious: 1. Impious; wicked. (old) "The life of the unpitous." Wyclif (Prov. xv. 8). 2. Destitute of pity; pitiless. (old) Chaucer. -- Un*pi"tous*ly, adv. (old) -- Un*pi"tous*ness, n. (old) Wyclif.
unform: To decompose, or resolve into parts; to destroy the form of; to unmake. Good.
underslung: Of an automobile body, suspended from the springs in such a manner that the frame of the chassis is below the axles, the object being to lower the center of gravity of the car.
unbottomed: 1. Etym: [1st pref. un- + bottom + -ed.] Deprived of a bottom. 2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + bottomed.] Having no bottom; bottomless. Milton.
unregenerate: Not regenerated; not renewed in heart; remaining or being at enmity with God.
undivided: 1. Not divided; not separated or disunited; unbroken; whole; continuous; as, plains undivided by rivers or mountains. 2. Not set off, as a share in a firm; not made actually separate by division; as, a partner, owning one half in a firm, is said to own an undivided half so long as the business continues and his share is not set off to him. 3.
unbashful: Not bashful or modest; bold; impudent; shameless. Shak.
unhumanize: To render inhuman or barbarous. J. Barlow.
unresty: Causing unrest; disquieting; as, unresty sorrows. (old) Chaucer.
unconversion: The state of being unconverted; impenitence.
unpartial: Impartial. (old) Bp. Sanderson. -- Un*par"tial*ly, adv. (old) Hooker.
unsting: To disarm of a sting; to remove the sting of. "Elegant dissertations on virtue and vice . . . will not unsting calamity." J. M. Mason.
unplained: Not deplored or bewailed; unlamented. (old) Spenser.
unsurety: Want of surety; uncertainty; insecurity; doubt. (old) Sir T. More.
unmannerly: Not mannerly; ill-bred; rude. -- adv. Uncivilly; rudely. -- Un*man"ner*li*ness, n.
uniformity: 1. The quality or state of being uniform; freedom from variation or difference; resemblance to itself at all times; sameness of action, effect, etc., under like conditions; even tenor; as, the uniformity of design in a poem; the uniformity of nature. 2. Consistency; sameness; as, the uniformity of a man's opinions. 3. Similitude between the parts of a whole;
unimpairable: That can not be impaired. Hakewill.
unhorse: To throw from a horse; to cause to dismount; also, to take a horse or horses from; as, to unhorse a rider; to unhorse a carriage. Cowper.
unchristened: Not christened; as, an unchristened child.
unslaked: Not slaked; unslacked; as, an unslaked thirst; unslaked lime.
uncunning: Ignorant. (old) I am young and uncunning, as thou wost [knowest]. Chaucer.
unguiculata: An extensive division of Mammalia including those having claws or nails, as distinguished from the hoofed animals (Ungulata).
underpinning: 1. The act of one who underpins; the act of supporting by stones, masonry, or the like. 2. (Arch.) (a) That by which a building is underpinned; the material and construction used for support, introduced beneath a wall already constructed. (b) The foundation, esp. of a frame house. [Local, U.S.]
unkiss: To cancel or annul what was done or sealed by a kiss; to cancel by a kiss. (old) Let me unkiss the oath 'twixt thee and me. Shak.
untwine: To untwist; to separate, as that which is twined or twisted; to disentangle; to untie. It requires a long and powerful counter sympathy in a nation to untwine the ties of custom which bind a people to the established and the old. Sir W. Hamilton.
unchristianly: Unchristian. Milton. | In an unchristian manner.
understock: To supply insufficiently with stock. A. Smith.
