underproof: Containing less alcohol than proof spirit. See Proof spirit, under Spirit.
unwarp: To restore from a warped state; to cause to be linger warped.
untoward: 1. Froward; perverse. "Save yourselves from this untoward generation." Acts ii. 40. 2. Awkward; ungraceful. "Untoward words." Creech. "Untoward manner." Swift. 3. Inconvenient; troublesome; vexatious; unlucky; unfortunate; as, an untoward wind or accident. -- Un*to"ward*ly, adv. -- Un*to"ward*ness, n.
unriddle: To read the riddle of; to solve or explain; as, to unriddle an enigma or a mystery. Macaulay. And where you can't unriddle, learn to trust. Parnell.
underlaborer: An assistant or subordinate laborer. Locke.
uncontrollable: 1. Incapable of being controlled; ungovernable; irresistible; as, an uncontrollable temper; uncontrollable events. 2. Indisputable; irrefragable; as, an uncontrollable maxim; an uncontrollable title. Swift. -- Un`con*trol"la*ble*ness, n. -- Un`con*trol"la*bly, adv.
unembodied: 1. Free from a corporeal body; disembodied; as, unembodied spirits. Byron. 2. Not embodied; not collected into a body; not yet organized; as, unembodied militia.
unmould: To change the form of; to reduce from any form. "Unmolding reason's mintage." Milton.
unco: Unknown; strange, or foreign; unusual, or surprising; distant in manner; reserved. [Scot.] | In a high degree; to a great extent; greatly; very. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
unbridled: Loosed from the bridle, or as from the bridle; hence, unrestrained; licentious; violent; as, unbridled passions. "Unbridled boldness." B. Jonson. Lands deluged by unbridled floods. Wordsworth. -- Un*bri"dled*ness, n. Abp. Leighton.
undersuit: A suit worn under another suit; a suit of underclothes.
undersong: 1. The burden of a song; the chorus; the refrain. Dryden. 2. Accompanying strain; subordinate and underlying meaning; accompaniment; undertone. In the very [poetry] there often an undersong of sense which none beside the poetic mind . . . can comprehend. Landor.
unilabiate: Having one lip only; as, a unilabiate corolla.
uncling: To cease from clinging or adhering. (old) Milton.
unstop: 1. To take the stopple or stopper from; as, to unstop a bottle or a cask. 2. To free from any obstruction; to open.
unacquainted: 1. Not acquainted. Cowper. 2. Not usual; unfamiliar; strange. (old) And the unacquainted light began to fear. Spenser.
unformed: 1. Decomposed, or resolved into parts; having the form destroyed. 2. Not formed; not arranged into regular shape, order, or relations; shapeless; amorphous. 3. (Biol.) Unorganized; without definite shape or structure; as, an unformed, or unorganized, ferment. Unformed stars (Astron.), stars not grouped into any constellation; informed stars. See Sporades.
unbeseeming: Unbecoming; not befitting. -- Un`be*seem"ing*ly, adv. -- Un`be*seem"ing*ness, n.
underprop: To prop from beneath; to put a prop under; to support; to uphold. Underprop the head that bears the crown. Fenton.
unequal: 1. Not equal; not matched; not of the same size, length, breadth, quantity, strength, talents, acquirements, age, station, or the like; as, the fingers are of unequal length; peers and commoners are unequal in rank. 2. Ill balanced or matched; disproportioned; hence, not equitable; partial; unjust; unfair. Against unequal arms to fight in pain. Milton.
ungenerous: Not generous; illiberal; ignoble; unkind; dishonorable. The victor never will impose on Cato Ungenerous terms. Addison.
unnecessary: Not necessary; not required under the circumstances; unless; needless; as, unnecessary labor, care, or rigor. -- Un*nec"es*sa*ri*ly, adv. -- Un*nec"es*sa*ri*ness, n.
untongue: To deprive of a tongue, or of voice. (old) Fuller.
unmeaning: 1. Having no meaning or signification; as, unmeaning words. 2. Not indicating intelligence or sense; senseless; expressionless; as, an unmeaning face. There pride sits blazoned on the unmeaning brow. Trumbull. -- Un*mean"ing*ly, adv. -- Un*mean"ing*ness, n.
understandable: Capable of being understood; intelligible. Chillingworth.
unsuffering: Inability or incapability of enduring, or of being endured. (old) Wyclif.
unsheriff: To depose from the office of sheriff.
unbenevolence: Absence or want of benevolence; ill will.
untruss: To loose from a truss, or as from a truss; to untie or unfasten; to let out; to undress. Dryden. | One who untrussed persons for the purpose of flogging them; a public whipper. (old) B. Jonson.
underloadstarter: A motor starter provided with an underload switch.
unbowed: Not bent or arched; not bowed down. Byron.
unmoneyed: Destitute of money; not rich. [Written also unmonied.] Shenstone.
unweld: Unwieldy; unmanageable; clumsy. (old) Our old limbs move [may] well be unweld. Chaucer.
unwashen: Not washed. (old) "To eat with unwashen hands." Matt. xv. 20.
unction: 1. The act of anointing, smearing, or rubbing with an unguent, oil, or ointment, especially for medical purposes, or as a symbol of consecration; as, mercurial unction. To be heir, and to be king By sacred unction, thy deserved right. Milton. 2. That which is used for anointing; an unguent; an ointment; hence, anything soothing or lenitive.
unaccountable: 1. Not accountable or responsible; free from control. South. 2. Not to be accounted for; inexplicable; not consonant with reason or rule; strange; mysterious. -- Un`ac*count"a*ble*ness}, n. -- Un`ac*count"a*bly, adv.
unking: To cause to cease to be a king. Shall his condescension, therefore, unking him South.
untighten: To make less tight or tense; to loosen.
unnature: To change the nature of; to invest with a different or contrary nature. (old) A right heavenly nature, indeed, as if were unnaturing them, doth so bridle them [the elements]. Sir P. Sidney. | The contrary of nature; that which is unnatural. So as to be rather unnature, after all, than nature. H. Bushnell.
unpeerable: Incapable of having a peer, or equal.
unshapen: Not shaped; shapeless; misshapen; deformed; ugly.
uncaused: Having no antecedent cause; uncreated; self-existent; eternal. A. Baxter.
unicity: The condition of being united; quality of the unique; unification. Not unity, but what the schoolmen call unicity. De Quincey. The unicity we strive not to express, for that is impossible, but to designate by the nearest analogy. Coleridge.
untowardly: Perverse; froward; untoward. "Untowardly tricks and vices." Locke.
unbalanced: 1. Not balanced; not in equipoise; having no counterpoise, or having insufficient counterpoise. Let Earth unbalanced from her orbit fly. Pope. 2. (Com.) Not adjusted; not settled; not brought to an equality of debt and credit; as, an unbalanced account; unbalanced books. 3. Being, or being thrown, out of equilibrium; hence, disordered or deranged in sense; unsteady; unsound;
unlocated: 1. Not located or placed; not fixed in a place. 2. Not surveyed, or designated by marks, limits, or boundaries, as appropriated to some individual, company, or corporation; as, unlocated lands.
unsensualize: To elevate from the domain of the senses; to purify. Coleridge.
under: 1. Below or lower, in place or position, with the idea of being covered; lower than; beneath; -- opposed to over; as, he stood under a tree; the carriage is under cover; | In a lower, subject, or subordinate condition; in subjection; - - used chiefly in a few idiomatic phrases; as, to bring under, to reduce to subjection; to subdue;
undertenancy: Tenancy or tenure under a tenant or lessee; the tenure of an undertenant.
underline: 1. To mark a line below, as words; to underscore. 2. To influence secretly. (old) Sir H. Wotton.
unripeness: Quality or state of being unripe.
unheired: Destitute of an heir. To leave him utterly unheired. Chapman.
unpolicied: 1. Not having civil polity, or a regular form of government. 2. Impolitic; imprudent. (old) Shak.
unthinking: 1. Not thinking; not heedful; thoughtless; inconsiderate; as, unthinking youth. 2. Not indicating thought or reflection; thoughtless. With earnest eyes, and round unthinking face, He first the snuffbox opened, then the case. Pope. -- Un*think"ing*ly, adv. -- Un*think"ing*ness, n.
unparliamentary: Not parliamentary; contrary to the practice of parliamentary bodies. -- Un*par`lia*men"ta*ri*ness, n.
unguiform: Having the form of a claw or claws.
unavoidable: 1. Not avoidable; incapable of being shunned or prevented; inevitable; necessary; as, unavoidable troubles. 2. (Law) Not voidable; incapable of being made null or void. Blackstone. Unavoidable hemorrhage (Med.), hemorrhage produced by the afterbirth, or placenta, being situated over the mouth of the womb so as to require detachment before the child can be born.
unsuccessful: Not successful; not producing the desired event; not fortunate; meeting with, or resulting in, failure; unlucky; unhappy. -- Un`suc*cess"ful*ly, adv. -- Un`suc*cess"ful*ness, n.
undisclose: To keep close or secret. (old) Daniel.
unlived: Bereft or deprived of life. (old) Shak.
ungulate: 1. Shaped like a hoof. 2. (Zoöl.) Furnished with hoofs. See the Note under Nail, n., 1. | Any hoofed quadruped; one of the Ungulata.
unemployed: 1. Nor employed in manual or other labor; having no regular work. 2. Not invested or used; as, unemployed capital.
undulatory: Moving in the manner of undulations, or waves; resembling the motion of waves, which successively rise or swell rise or swell and fall; pertaining to a propagated alternating motion, similar to that of waves.
unget: To cause to be unbegotten or unborn, or as if unbegotten or unborn. I 'll disown you, I 'll disinherit you, I 'll unget you. Sheridan.
undershot: 1. (Zoöl.) Having the lower incisor teeth projecting beyond the upper ones, as in the bulldog. 2. Moved by water passing beneath; -- said of a water wheel, and opposed to overshot; as, an undershot wheel.
untreatable: Incapable of being treated; not practicable. Dr. H. More.
underfeed: To feed with too little food; to supply with an insufficient quantity of food.
undefine: To make indefinite; to obliterate or confuse the definition or limitations of.
unpriest: To deprive of priesthood; to unfrock. Milton.
unheard: 1. Not heard; not perceived by the ear; as, words unheard by those present. 2. Not granted an audience or a hearing; not allowed to speak; not having made a defense, or stated one's side of a question; disregarded; unheeded; as, to condemunheard. What pangs I feel, unpitied and unheard! Dryden. 3. Not known to fame; not illustrious or celebrated; obscure.
unthrone: To remove from, or as from, a throne; to dethrone. Milton.
unbidden: 1. Not bidden; not commanded. Thorns also and thistles it shall bring thee forth Unbid; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field. Milton. 2. Uninvited; as, unbidden guests. Shak. 3. Being without a prayer. (old) Spenser.
unruinated: Not ruined or destroyed. (old) "Unruinated towers." Bp. Hall.
undull: To remove the dullness of; to clear. (old) Whitlock.
underpin: 1. To lay stones, masonry, etc., under, as the sills of a building, on which it is to rest. 2. To support by some solid foundation; to place something underneath for support.
underrun: To run or pass under; especially (Naut.), to pass along and under, as a cable, for the purpose of taking it in, or of examining it. Note: The cable passes over the bows and stern of the boat used, while the men haul the boat along by pulling upon the cable. Totten. To underrun a tackle (Naut.), to separate its parts and put them in order.
unbeguile: To set free from the influence of guile; to undeceive. "Then unbeguile thyself." Donne.
unreaved: Not torn, split, or parted; not torn to pieces. (old) Bp. Hall.
unpossess: To be without, or to resign, possession of. (old)
unce: An ounce; a small portion. (old) "By unces hung his locks." Chaucer.
undauntable: Incapable of being daunted; intrepid; fearless; indomitable. Bp. Hall.
unsphere: To remove, as a planet, from its sphere or orb. Shak.
unsubstantial: Lacking in matter or substance; visionary; chimerical.
unsuccess: Want of success; failure; misfortune. Prof. Wilson.
untrammeled: Not hampered or impeded; free. [Written also untrammelled.]
unstable: Not stable; not firm, fixed, or constant; subject to change or overthrow. -- Un*sta"ble*ness, n. Chaucer. Unstable equilibrium. See Stable equilibrium, under Stable.
unshot: To remove the shot from, as from a shotted gun; to unload. | Not hit by a shot; also, not discharged or fired off.
uniaxial: 1. (Crystallog.) Having but one optic axis, or line of no double refraction. Note: In uniaxial crystals, the optic axis has the direction of the vertical crystallographic axis. All tetragonal and hexagonal crystals are uniaxial. 2. (Biol.) Having only one axis; developing along a single line or plane; -- opposed to multiaxial.
unalmsed: Not having received alms. [Obs. & R.] Pollock.
unproselyte: To convert or recover from the state of a proselyte. Fuller.
underground: The place or space beneath the surface of the ground; subterranean space. A spirit raised from depth of underground. Shak. | 1. Being below the surface of the ground; as, an underground story or apartment. 2. Done or occurring out of sight; secret. [Colloq.] Underground railroad or railway. See under Railroad.
unvaluable: 1. Invaluable; being beyond price. (old) South. 2. Not valuable; having little value. T. Adams.
unfair: To deprive of fairness or beauty. Shak. | Not fair; not honest; not impartial; disingenuous; using or involving trick or artifice; dishonest; unjust; unequal. You come, like an unfair merchant, to charge me with being in your debt. Swift.
unspike: To remove a spike from, as from the vent of a cannon.
uncheckable: Not capable of being checked or stopped.
unconditioned: 1. Not conditioned or subject to conditions; unconditional. 2. (Metaph.) Not subject to condition or limitations; infinite; absolute; hence, inconceivable; incogitable. Sir W. Hamilton. The unconditioned (Metaph.), all that which is inconceivable and beyond the realm of reason; whatever is inconceivable under logical forms or relations.
unencumber: To free from incumbrance; to disencumber.
unhappy: 1. Not happy or fortunate; unfortunate; unlucky; as, affairs have taken an unhappy turn. 2. In a degree miserable or wretched; not happy; sad; sorrowful; as, children render their parents unhappy by misconduct. 3. Marked by infelicity; evil; calamitous; as, an unhappy day. "The unhappy morn." Milton. 4. Mischievous; wanton; wicked. (old) Shak. -- Un*hap"pi*ly, adv.
uncivilization: The state of being uncivilized; savagery or barbarism.
unfeatured: Wanting regular features; deformed. "Visage rough, deformed, unfeatured, and a skin of buff." Dryden.
unnotify: To retract or withdraw a notice of. Walpole.
univocally: In a univocal manner; in one term; in one sense; not equivocally. How is sin univocally distinguished into venial and mortal, if the venial be not sin Bp. Hall.
unparagoned: Having no paragon or equal; matchless; peerless. Your unparagoned mistress is dead. Shak.
undergroan: To groan beneath. (old) Earth undergroaned their high-raised feet. Chapman.
unpicked: Picked out; picked open. 2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + picked.] Not picked. Milton.
unapparel: To divest of clothing; to strip. (old) Donne.
unwarrantable: Not warrantable; indefensible; not vindicable; not justifiable; illegal; unjust; improper. -- Un*war"rant*a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*war"rant*a*bly, adv.
unbutton: To loose the buttons of; to unfasten.
unipersonalist: One who believes that the Deity is unipersonal.
unquiet: To disquiet. (old) Ld. Herbert. | Not quiet; restless; uneasy; agitated; disturbed. -- Un*qui"et*ly, adv. -- Un*qui"et*ness, n.
uncircumcised: Not circumcised; hence, not of the Israelites. "This uncircumcised Philistine." 1 Sam. xvii. 26.
unwarranted: Not warranted; being without warrant, authority, or guaranty; unwarrantable.
unprop: To remove a prop or props from; to deprive of support.
unphilosophize: To degrade from the character of a philosopher. Pope.
unsin: To deprive of sinfulness, as a sin; to make sinless. (old) Feltham.
unadvisable: Not advisable; inadvisable; inexpedient. Lowth. -- Un`ad*vis"a*bly, adv.
unconstancy: Inconstancy. (old) "The unconstancy of the foundation." Fuller.
unsaturation: The quality or state of being unsaturated.
unlimber: To detach the limber from; as, to unlimber a gun.
unsluice: To sluice; to open the sluice or sluices of; to let flow; to discharge. Dryden.
unwork: To undo or destroy, as work previously done.
unfrequent: Infrequent. J. H. Newman. -- Un*fre"quent*ly adv. | To cease to frequent. (old) They quit their thefts and unfrequent the fields. J. Philips.
unit: 1. A single thing or person. 2. (Arith.) The least whole number; one. Units are the integral parts of any large number. I. Watts. 3. A gold coin of the reign of James I., of the value of twenty shillings. Camden. 4. Any determinate amount or quantity (as of length, time, heat, value) adopted as a standard of measurement for other amounts or quantities of the same kind. 5.
unreasoned: Not supported by reason; unreasonable. "Unreasoned habits." Burke.
unsuspicion: The quality or state of being unsuspecting. Dickens.
unmuffle: 1. To take a covering from, as the face; to uncover. 2. To remove the muffling of, as a drum.
unusual: Not usual; uncommon; rare; as, an unusual season; a person of unusual grace or erudition. -- Un*u"su*al*ly, adv. -- Un*u"su*al*ness, n.
untempter: One who does not tempt, or is not a tempter. (old) Wyclif.
unstitch: To open by picking out stitches; to take out, or undo, the stitches of; as, to unstitch a seam. Collier.
unpray: To revoke or annul by prayer, as something previously prayed for. Sir M. Hale.
un: An inseparable verbal prefix or particle. It is prefixed: (a) To verbs to express the contrary, and not the simple negative, of the action of the verb to which it is prefixed; | An inseparable prefix, or particle, signifying not; in-; non-. In- is prefixed mostly to words of Latin origin, or else to words formed by Latin suffixes; un- is of much wider application, and is…
underlayer: 1. One who, or that which, underlays or is underlaid; a lower layer. 2. (Mining) A perpendicular shaft sunk to cut the lode at any required depth. Weale.
unexpected: Not expected; coming without warning; sudden. -- Un`ex*pect"ed*ly, adv. -- Un`ex*pect"ed*ness, n.
unfree: Not free; held in bondage. There had always been a slave class, a class of the unfree, among the English as among all German peoples. J. R. Green
unmember: To deprive of membership, as in a church.
untune: To make incapable of harmony, or of harmonious action; to put out of tune. Shak.
unbooked: Not written in a book; unrecorded. "UnbookedEnglish life." Masson.
unproficiency: Want of proficiency or improvement. Bp. Hall.
unblest: Not blest; excluded from benediction; hence, accursed; wretched. "Unblessed enchanter." Milton.
unseasonable: Not seasonable; being, done, or occurring out of the proper season; ill-timed; untimely; too early or too late; as, he called at an unseasonable hour; unseasonable advice; unseasonable frosts; unseasonable food. -- Un*sea"son*a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*sea"son*a*bly, adv.
underbrace: To brace, fasten, or bind underneath or below. Cowper.
unharbored: 1. Having no harbor or shelter; unprotected. 2. Affording no harbor or shelter. "Unharbored heaths." (old) Milton.
uniocular: Of, pertaining to, or seated in, one eye; monocular.
unfriendly: 1. Not friendly; not kind or benevolent; hostile; as, an unfriendly neighbor. 2. Not favorable; not adapted to promote or support any object; as, weather unfriendly to health. -- Un*friend"li*ness, n.
unstack: To remove, or take away, from a stack; to remove, as something constituting a stack.
universology: The science of the universe, and the relations which it involves.
unset: Not set; not fixed or appointed.
unaidable: Incapable of being aided. "Her unaidable estate." Shak.
unconcernment: The state of being unconcerned, or of having no share or concern; unconcernedness. (old) South.
unpolish: To deprive of polish; to make impolite.
unlawlike: Not according to law; being or done in violation of law; unlawful. Milton.
unctuous: 1. Of the nature or quality of an unguent or ointment; fatty; oily; greasy. "The unctuous cheese." Longfellow. 2. Having a smooth, greasy feel, as certain minerals. 3. Bland; suave; also, tender; fervid; as, an unctuous speech; sometimes, insincerely suave or fervid. -- Unc"tu*ous*ly, adv. -- Unc"tu*ous*ness, n.
underhonest: Not entirely honest. "We think him overproud and underhonest." Shak.
unrumple: To free from rumples; to spread or lay even,
unreverence: Absence or lack of reverence; irreverence. (old) Wyclif.
unblessed: Not blest; excluded from benediction; hence, accursed; wretched. "Unblessed enchanter." Milton.
unatonable: 1. Not capable of being brought into harmony; irreconcilable. "Unatonable matrimony." (old) Milton. 2. Incapable of being atoned for; inexpiable.
unforesee: To fail to foresee. Bp. Hacket.
unglorify: To deprive of glory. I. Watts.
unbrewed: Not made by brewing; unmixed; pure; genuine. Young.
unfellow: To prevent from being a fellow or companion; to separate from one's fellows; to dissever. Death quite unfellows us. Mrs. Browning.
unprobably: In a manner not to be approved of; improperly. [Obs. & R.] To diminish, by the authority of wise and knowing men, things unjustly and unprobably crept in. Strype.
unowned: 1. Not owned; having no owner. Milton. 2. Not acknowledged; not avowed. Gay.
unwedgeable: Not to be split with wedges. (old) Shak.
unbiased: Free from bias or prejudice; unprejudiced; impartial. -- Un*bi"ased*ness, n.
unthriftfully: Not thriftily. (old) "Unthriftfully spent." Sir J. Cheke.
undock: To take out of dock; as, to undock a ship.
unmade: 1. Etym: [Pref. un- not + made.] Not yet made or formed; as, an unmade grave. Shak. 2. Etym: [Properly p. p. of unmake.] Deprived of form, character, etc.; disunited.
unmerchantable: Not merchantable; not fit for market; being of a kind, quality, or quantity that is unsalable. McElrath.
unstockinged: 1. Etym: [Pref. un- not + stocking.] Destitute of stockings. Sir W. Scott. 2. Etym: [1st pref. un- + stocking.] Deprived of stockings.
unmake: To destroy the form and qualities of; to deprive of being; to uncreate. God does not make or unmake things to try experiments. T. Burnet.
unripe: 1. Not ripe; as, unripe fruit. 2. Developing too early; premature. Sir P. Sidney.
ungifted: Being without gifts, especially native gifts or endowments. Cowper.
unseminared: Deprived of virility, or seminal energy; made a eunuch. (old)
underfoot: Under the feet; underneath; below. See Under foot, under Foot, n. | Low; base; abject; trodden down.
unanimous: 1. Being of one mind; agreeing in opinion, design, or determination; consentient; not discordant or dissentient; harmonious; as, the assembly was unanimous; the members of the council were unanimous. "Both in one faith unanimous." Milton. 2. Formed with unanimity; indicating unanimity; having the agreement and consent of all;
unpassable: Impassable. E. A. Freeman. -- Un*pass"a*ble*ness, n. Evelyn.
uncloak: To remove a cloak or cover from; to deprive of a cloak or cover; to unmask; to reveal. | To remove, or take off, one's cloak.
unlooked: Not observed or foreseen; unexpected; -- generally with for. "Unlooked success." Denham. She comes unlooked for, if she comes at all. Pope.
unprelated: Deposed from the office of prelate.
uncivilized: 1. Not civilized; not reclaimed from savage life; rude; barbarous; savage; as, the uncivilized inhabitants of Central Africa. 2. Not civil; coarse; clownish. Addison.
underbid: To bid less than, as when a contract or service is offered to the lowest bidder; to offer to contract, sell, or do for a less price than.
uncharity: Uncharitableness. Tennyson. 'T were much uncharity in you. J. Webster.
unlatch: To open or loose by lifting the latch; as, to unlatch a door.
underhew: To hew less than is usual or proper; specifically, to hew, as a piece of timber which should be square, in such a manner that it appears to contain a greater number of cubic feet than it really does contain. Haldeman.
unready: 1. Not ready or prepared; not prompt; slow; awkward; clumsy. Dryden. Nor need the unready virgin strike her breast. Keble. 2. Not dressed; undressed. (old) | To undress. (old) Sir P. Sidney.
unglove: To take off the glove or gloves of; as, to unglove the hand. Beau. & Fl.
unplume: To strip of plumes or feathers; hence, to humiliate.
undertone: A low or subdued tone or utterance; a tone less loud than usual.
unchancy: 1. Happening at a bad time; unseasonable; inconvenient. A. Trollope. 2. Ill-fated; unlucky. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.] 3. Unsafe to meddle with; dangerous. [Scot.]
unnun: To remove from condition of being a nun. Many did quickly unnun and disfriar themselves. Fuller.
unlovely: Not lovely; not amiable; possessing qualities that excite dislike; disagreeable; displeasing; unpleasant. -- Un*love"li*ness, n.
ungrave: To raise or remove from the grave; to disinter; to untomb; to exhume. (old) Fuller.
ungird: To loose the girdle or band of; to unbind; to unload. He ungirded his camels. Gen. xxiv. 32.
unfrankable: Not frankable; incapable of being sent free by public conveyance.
unlute: To separate, as things cemented or luted; to take the lute or the clay from. Boyle.
unpaired: Not paired; not suited or matched. And minds unpaired had better think alone. Crabbe.
unlink: To separate or undo, as links; to uncoil; to unfasten. Shak.
unwild: To tame; to subdue. [Obs. & R.] Sylvester.
unlawed: Not having the claws and balls of the forefeet cut off; -- said of dogs.
uniphonous: Having but one sound, as the drum.
unmiter: To deprive of a miter; to depose or degrade from the rank of a bishop. Milton.
unequity: Want of equity or uprightness; injustice; wickedness; iniquity. (old) Wyclif.
unshipment: The act of unshipping, or the state of being unshipped; displacement.
unsettle: To move or loosen from a settled position or state; to unfix; to displace; to disorder; to confuse. | To become unsettled or unfixed; to be disordered. Shak.
universalize: To make universal; to generalize. Coleridge.
ungear: To strip of gear; to unharness; to throw out of gear.
unteam: To unyoke a team from. Jer. Taylor.
underglaze: Applied under the glaze, that is, before the glaze, that is, before the glaze is put on; fitted to be so applied; -- said of colors in porcelain painting.
unamiable: Not amiable; morose; ill-natured; repulsive. -- Un*a"mi*a*bly, adv.
unhonest: Dishonest; dishonorable. Ascham. -- Un*hon"est*ly, adv. Udall.
uncurse: To free from a curse or an execration. Shak.
unshape: To deprive of shape, or of proper shape; to disorder; to confound; to derange. Shak.
undam: To free from a dam, mound, or other obstruction. Dryden.
undue: 1. Not due; not yet owing; as, an undue debt, note, or bond. 2. Not right; not lawful or legal; improper; as, an undue proceeding. Bacon. 3. Not agreeable to a rule or standard, or to duty; disproportioned; excessive; immoderate; inordinate; as, an undue attachment to forms; an undue rigor in the execution of law.
unnatural: Not natural; contrary, or not conforming, to the order of nature; being without natural traits; as, unnatural crimes. Syn. -- See Factitious. -- Un*nat"u*ral*ly, adv. -- Un*nat"u*ral*ness, n.
unequaled: Not equaled; unmatched; unparalleled; unrivaled; exceeding; surpassing; -- in a good or bad sense; as, unequaled excellence; unequaled ingratitude or baseness. [Written also unequalled.]
underproduction: The production of less than is demanded or of less than the usual supply. F. A. Walker.
unsling: To take off the slings of, as a yard, a cask, or the like; to release from the slings. Totten.
unincumbered: 1. Not incumbered; not burdened. 2. (Law) Free from any temporary estate or interest, or from mortgage, or other charge or debt; as, an estate unincumbered with dower.
universality: The quality or state of being universal; unlimited extension or application; generality; -- distinguished from particularity; as, the unversality of a proposition; the unversality of sin; the unversality of the Deluge.
uncovenable: Not covenable; inconvenient. (old) Wyclif (1 Tim. iv. 7).
unsimplicity: Absence of simplicity; artfulness. C. Kingsley.
uniformly: In a uniform manner; without variation or diversity; by a regular, constant, or common ratio of change; with even tenor; as, a temper uniformly mild. To vary uniformly (Math.), to vary with the ratio of the corresponding increments constant; -- said of two dependent quantities with regard to each other.
uninfringible: That may not be infringed; as, an uninfringible monopoly.
unharmonious: Inharmonious; unsymmetrical; also, unmusical; discordant. Swift. -- Un`har*mo"ni*ous*ly, adv.
uncoach: To detach or loose from a coach. (old) Chapman.
undulating: Rising and falling like waves; resembling wave form or motion; undulatory; rolling; wavy; as, an undulating medium; undulating ground. -- Un"du*la`ting*ly. adv.
undercoat: 1. A coat worn under another; a light coat, as distinguished from an overcoat, or a greatcoat. 2. A growth of short hair or fur partially concealed by a longer growth; as, a dog's undercoat.
unconcluding: Inconclusive. (old) Locke. -- Un`con*clud"ing*ness, n. (old) Jer. Taylor.
unflower: To strip of flowers. G. Fletcher.
unrelenting: Not relenting; unyielding; rigid; hard; stern; cruel. -- Un`re*lent"ing*ly, adv. -- Un`re*lent"ing*ness, n.
unruinate: Not ruined or destroyed. (old) "Unruinated towers." Bp. Hall.
unfraught: 1. Etym: [Pref. un- not + fraught.] Not fraught; not burdened. 2. Etym: [1st pref. un- + fraught.] Removed, as a burden; unloaded. P. Fletcher.
unruffled: Not ruffled or agitated; smooth; calm; tranquil; quiet. Calm and unruffled as a summer's sea. Addison.
unsely: Not blessed or happy; wretched; unfortunate. [Written also unsilly.] (old) Chaucer. -- Un*se"li*ness, n. (old) Chaucer.
unwrap: To open or undo, as what is wrapped or folded. Chaucer.
unicellular: Having, or consisting of, but a single cell; as, a unicellular organism.
underlaid: Laid or placed underneath; also, having something laid or lying underneath.
unsitting: Not sitting well; unbecoming. (old) "Unsitting words." Sir T. More.
uncipher: To decipher; as, to uncipher a letter. (old) Sir W. Temple.
uncreated: 1. Deprived of existence; annihilated. Beau. & Fl. 2. Not yet created; as, misery uncreated. Milton. 3. Not existing by creation; self-existent; eternal; as, God is an uncreated being. Locke.
unhingement: The act unhinging, or the state of being unhinged.
unrighteous: 1. Not righteous; evil; wicked; sinful; as, an unrighteous man. 2. Contrary to law and equity; unjust; as, an unrighteous decree or sentence. -- Un*right"eous*ly, adv. -- Un*right"eous*ness, n.
unclog: To disencumber of a clog, or of difficulties and obstructions; to free from encumbrances; to set at liberty. Shak.
undershut: Closed from beneath. Undershut valve (Mach.), a valve which shuts by being lifted against a seat facing downward. Knight.
unionist: 1. One who advocates or promotes union; especially a loyal supporter of a federal union, as that of the United States. 2. A member or supporter of a trades union.
unfeather: To deprive of feathers; to strip.
unhandy: Clumsy; awkward; as, an Unhandy man.
undergo: 1. To go or move below or under. (old) 2. To be subjected to; to bear up against; to pass through; to endure; to suffer; to sustain; as, to undergo toil and fatigue; to undergo pain, grief, or anxiety; to undergothe operation of amputation; food in the stomach undergoes the process of digestion. Certain to undergo like doom. Milton. 3. To be the bearer of; to possess.
unfinished: Not finished, not brought to an end; imperfect; incomplete; left in the rough; wanting the last hand or touch; as, an unfinished house; an unfinished picture; an unfinished iron casting.
unshakable: Not capable of being shaken; firm; fixed. Shak. J. S. Mill.
unsensed: Wanting a distinct meaning; having no certain signification. Puller.
unnooked: Without nooks and corners; guileless. (old) "Unnooked simplicity." Marston.
ungod: 1. To deprive of divinity; to undeify. Donne. 2. To cause to recognize no god; to deprive of a god; to make atheistical. Dryden.
uncity: To deprive of the rank or rights of a city. (old)
unconceivable: Inconceivable. (old) Locke. -- Un`con*ceiv"a*ble*ness, n. (old) -- Un`con*ceiv"a*bly, adv. (old)
uncreate: To deprive of existence; to annihilate. Who can uncreate thee, thou shalt know. Milton. | Uncreated; self-existent. Book of Common Prayer.
unked: 1. Odd; strange; ugly; old; uncouth. [Prov. Eng.] 2. Lonely; dreary; unkard. [Prov. Eng.] Weston is sadly unked without you. Cowper.
uncinate: Hooked; bent at the tip in the form of a hook; as, an uncinate process.
unwares: Unawares; unexpectedly; -- sometimes preceded by at. (old) Holinshed.
unprayable: Not to be influenced or moved by prayers; obdurate. Wyclif.
unreserve: Absence of reverse; frankness; freedom of communication. T. Warton.
unnapped: Finished without a nap. I did not attempt her with a threadbare name, Unnapped with meritorious actions. Beau. & Fl.
unfruitful: Not producing fruit or offspring; unproductive; infertile; barren; sterile; as, an unfruitful tree or animal; unfruitful soil; an unfruitful life or effort. -- Un*fruit"ful*ly, adv. -- Un*fruit"ful*ness, n.
undoer: One who undoes anything; especially, one who ruins another.
unexceptionable: Not liable to any exception or objection; unobjectionable; faultless; good; excellent; as, a man of most unexceptionable character. -- Un`ex*cep"tion*a*ble*ness, n. -- Un`ex*cep"tion*a*bly, adv. Chesterfield is an unexceptionable witness. Macaulay.
underset: To prop or support. Bacon. | Undercurrent.
unvisard: To take the vizard or mask from; to unmask. [Written also unvizard.] (old) Milton.
unearth: To drive or draw from the earth; hence, to uncover; to bring out from concealment; to bring to light; to disclose; as, to unearth a secret. To unearth the roof of an old tree. Wordsworth.
uncorruptible: Incorruptible. "The glory of the uncorruptible God." Rom. i. 23.
ungrateful: 1. Not grateful; not thankful for favors; making no returns, or making ill return for kindness, attention, etc.; ingrateful. South. 2. Unpleasing; unacceptable; disagreeable; as, harsh sounds are ungrateful to the ear. -- Un*grate"ful*ly, adv. -- Un*grate"ful*ness, n.
undertenant: The tenant of a tenant; one who holds lands or tenements of a tenant or lessee.
unbelieving: 1. Not believing; incredulous; doubting; distrusting; skeptical. 2. Believing the thing alleged no to be true; disbelieving; especially, believing that Bible is not a divine revelation, or that Christ was not a divine or a supernatural person. "Unbelieving Jews." Acts xiv. 2. -- Un`be*liev"ing*ly, adv. -- -- Un`be*liev"ing*ness, n.
uncanny: Not canny; unsafe; strange; weird; ghostly. Sir W. Scott. -- Un*can"ni*ness, n. G. Eliot.
unition: The act of uniting, or the state of being united; junction. (old) Wiseman.
ungive: To yield; to relax; to give way. (old)
unwarm: To lose warmth; to grow cold.
unexperienced: 1. Not experienced; being without experience; inexperienced. Swift. 2. Untried; -- applied to things. Cheyne.
unlearned: 1. Not learned; untaught; uneducated; ignorant; illiterate. 2. Not gained by study; not known. 3. Not exhibiting learning; as, unlearned verses. -- Un*learn"ed*ly, adv. -- Un*learn"ed*ness, n.
unsister: To separate, as sisters; to disjoin. [Poetic & R.] Tennyson.
unbosomer: One who unbosoms, or discloses. "An unbosomer of secrets." Thackeray.
untread: To tread back; to retrace. Shak.
unclothed: 1. Etym: [Properly p. p. of unclothe.] Divested or stripped of clothing. Byron. 2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + clothed.] Not yet clothed; wanting clothes; naked. -- Un*cloth"ed*ly, adv. (old) Bacon.
unke: A European aquatic toad (Bombinator igneus). Its back is dark; its belly is marked with crimson. Called also feuerkröte.
unturn: To turn in a reserve way, especially so as to open something; as, to unturn a key. Keats.
unforeskinned: Deprived of the foreskin; circumcised. Milton.
unapt: 1. Inapt; slow; dull. Bacon. 2. Unsuitable; unfit; inappropriate. Macaulay. 3. Not accustomed and not likely; not disposed. I am a soldier and unapt to weep. Shak. -- Un*apt"ly, adv. -- Un*apt"ness, n.
uncurtain: To remove a curtain from; to reveal. Moore.
unfleshly: Not pertaining to the flesh; spiritual.
untappice: to come out of concealment. (old) Massinger.
unbar: To remove a bar or bars from; to unbolt; to open; as, to unbar a gate. Heber.
unlade: 1. To take the load from; to take out the cargo of; as, to unlade a ship or a wagon. The venturous merchant . . . Shall here unlade him and depart no more. Dryden. 2. To unload; to remove, or to have removed, as a load or a burden; to discharge. There the ship was to unlade her burden. Acts. xxi. 3.
untruism: Something not true; a false statement. [Recent & R.] A. Trollope.
unblind: To free from blindness; to give or restore sight to; to open the eyes of. J. Webster (1607).
unbending: 1. Not bending; not suffering flexure; not yielding to pressure; stiff; -- applied to material things. Flies o'er unbending corn, and skims along the main. Pope. 2. Unyielding in will; not subject to persuasion or influence; inflexible; resolute; -- applied to persons. 3. Unyielding in nature; unchangeable; fixed; -- applied to abstract ideas; as, unbending truths. 4.
unwearied: Not wearied; not fatigued or tired; hence, persistent; not tiring or wearying; indefatigable. -- Un*wea"ried*ly, adv. -- Un*wea"ried*ness, n.
unsceptred: 1. Etym: [Pref. un- not + sceptered.] Having no scepter. 2. Etym: [1st pref. un- + scepter.] Deprived of a scepter.
underact: To perform inefficiently, as a play; to act feebly.
unballast: To free from ballast; to discharge ballast from. Totten. | Not ballasted. [Obs. & R.] Addison.
unreason: Want of reason; unreasonableness; absurdity. Abbot of Unreason. See Abbot of Misrule, under Abbot. | To undo, disprove, or refute by reasoning. (old) To unreason the equity of God's proceedings. South.
underbuy: To buy at less than the real value or worth; to buy cheaper than. J. Fletcher.
unionism: 1. The sentiment of attachment to a federal union, especially to the federal union of the United States. 2. The principles, or the system, of combination among workmen engaged in the same occupation or trade.
unalist: An ecclesiastical who holds but one benefice; -- distinguished from pluralist. [Eng.] V. Knox.
unvoweled: Having no vowel sounds or signs. [Written also unvowelled.] Skinner.
unseven: To render other than seven; to make to be no longer seven. [Obs. & R.] "To unseven the sacraments of the church of Rome." Fuller.
unlove: To cease to love; to hate. (old)
uncord: To release from cords; to loosen the cord or cords of; to unfasten or unbind; as, to uncord a package.
unsophisticated: Not sophisticated; pure; innocent; genuine. -- Un`so*phis"ti*ca`ted*ness, n.
unsociability: The quality or state of being unsociable; unsociableness.
unbelt: To remove or loose the belt of; to ungird.
unsound: Not sound; not whole; not solid; defective; infirm; diseased. -- Un*sound"ly, adv. -- Un*sound"ness, n.
unsearchable: Not searchable; inscrutable; hidden; mysterious. The counsels of God are to us unsearchable. Rogers. -- Un*search"a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*search"a*bly, adv.
undershrieve: A low shrub; a woody plant of low stature.
unclose: 1. To open; to separate the parts of; as, to unclose a letter; to unclose one's eyes. 2. To disclose; to lay open; to reveal.
unguicular: Of or pertaining to a claw or a nail; ungual.
unitarian: 1. (Theol.) One who denies the doctrine of the Trinity, believing that God exists only in one person; a unipersonalist; also, one of a denomination of Christians holding this belief. 2. | Of or pertaining to Unitarians, or their doctrines.
unshutter: To open or remove the shutters of. T. Hughes.
unsight: Doing or done without sight; not seeing or examining. [Colloq.] Unsight unseen, a colloquial phrase, denoting unseeing unseen, or unseen repeated; as, to buy a thing unsight unseen, that is, without seeing it. For to subscribe, unsight, unseen, To a new church discipline. Hudibras.
univalve: A shell consisting of one valve only; a mollusk whose shell is composed of a single piece, as the snails and conchs. Note: Most univalves are spiral and are the shells of gastropods, but many belong… | Having one valve; as, a univalve shell or pericarp.
unshut: To open, or throw open. (old) Chaucer.
unitize: To reduce to a unit, or one whole; to form into a unit; to unify.
unusage: Want or lack of usage. (old) Chaucer.
unpleasant: Not pleasant; not amiable or agreeable; displeasing; offensive. -- Un*pleas"ant*ly, adv. -- Un*pleas"ant*ness, n.
underkingdom: A subordinate or dependent kingdom. Tennyson.
uncongeal: To thaw; to become liquid again. Tennyson.
untrunked: Separated from its trunk or stock. (old)
unfriendship: The state or quality of being unfriendly; unfriendliness; enmity. An act of unfriendship to my sovereign person. Sir W. Scott.
uncourtliness: Absence of courtliness; rudeness; rusticity. Addison.
undo: 1. To reverse, as what has been done; to annul; to bring to naught. What's done can not be undone. Shak. To-morrow, ere the setting sun, She 'd all undo that she had done. Swift. 2. To loose; to open; to take to piece; to unfasten; to untie; hence, to unravel; to solve; as, to undo a knot; to undo a puzzling question; to undo a riddle. Tennyson. Pray you, undo this button.
unleavened: Not leavened; containing no leaven; as, unleavened bread.
univalved: Having one valve; as, a univalve shell or pericarp.
undoubted: Not doubted; not called in question; indubitable; indisputable; as, undoubted proof; undoubted hero. -- Un*doubt"ed*ly, adv.
unessential: 1. Not essential; not of prime importance; not indispensable; unimportant. Addison. 2. Void of essence, or real being. Milton. | Something not constituting essence, or something which is not of absolute necessity; as, forms are among the unessentials of religion.
ungotten: 1. Not gotten; not acquired. 2. Not begotten. [Obs. or Poetic] "His loins yet full of ungot princes." Waller.
undersetting: Something set or built under as a support; a pedestal. Sir H. Wotton.
unlikely: 1. Not likely; improbable; not to be reasonably expected; as, an unlikely event; the thing you mention is very unlikely. 2. Not holding out a prospect of success; likely to fail; unpromising; as, unlikely means. Hooker. 3. Not such as to inspire liking; unattractive; disagreeable. (old) "The unlikely eld of me." Chaucer.
unchaste: Not chaste; not continent; lewd. -- Un*chaste"ly, adv. -- Un*chaste"ness, n.
uneth: With difficulty; scarcely. See Uneath. [Written also unethe, unneth, unnethe, unnethes, etc.] (old) Chaucer.
unable: Not able; not having sufficient strength, means, knowledge, skill, or the like; impotent' weak; helpless; incapable; -- now usually followed by an infinitive or an adverbial phrase; as, unable for work; unable to bear fatigue. Sapless age and weak unable limbs. Shak.
unbefool: To deliver from the state of a fool; to awaken the mind of; to undeceive.
undirected: 1. Not directed; not guided; left without direction. 2. Not addressed; not superscribed, as a letter. 3. Misdirected; misled; led astray.
underhand: 1. Secret; clandestine; hence, mean; unfair; fraudulent. Addison. 2. (Baseball, Cricket, etc.) Done, as pitching, with the hand lower than the shoulder, or, as bowling, with the hand lower than elbow. | 1. By secret means; in a clandestine manner; hence, by fraud; unfairly. Such mean revenge, committed underhand. Dryden. Baillie Macwheeble provided Janet, underhand, with meal for their maintenance.
undertime: The under or after part of the day; undermeal; evening. (old) He, coming home at undertime, there found The fairest creature that he ever saw. Spenser.
unisonant: Being in unison; having the same degree of gravity or acuteness; sounded alike in pitch.
unitary: 1. Of or pertaining to a unit or units; relating to unity; as, the unitary method in arithmetic. 2. Of the nature of a unit; not divided; united. Unitary theory (Chem.), the modern theory that the molecules of all complete compounds are units, whose parts are bound together in definite structure, with mutual and reciprocal influence on each other, and are not mere aggregations…
uncock: 1. To let down the cock of, as a firearm. 2. To deprive of its cocked shape, as a hat, etc. 3. To open or spread from a cock or heap, as hay.
unpeace: Absence or lack of peace. (old) Testament of Love.
unification: The act of unifying, or the state of being unified. Unification with God was the final aim of the Neoplatonicians. Fleming.
undercroft: A subterranean room of any kind; esp., one under a church (see Crypt), or one used as a chapel or for any sacred purpose.
unerring: Committing no mistake; incapable or error or failure certain; sure; unfailing; as, the unerring wisdom of God. Hissing in air the unerring weapon flew. Dryden.
uncustomed: Uncustomable; also, not having paid duty or customs. Smollett.
underkeeper: A subordinate keeper or guardian. Gray.
unnear: Not near; not close to; at a distance from. (old) Davies (Muse's Sacrifice).
unringed: Not having a ring, as in the nose. "Pigs unringed." Hudibras.
undergraduateship: The position or condition of an undergraduate.
unconverted: 1. Not converted or exchanged. 2. Not changed in opinion, or from one faith to another. Specifically: -- (a) Not persuaded of the truth of the Christian religion; heathenish. Hooker. (b) Unregenerate; sinful; impenitent. Baxter.
unhasp: To unloose the hasp of; to unclose.
unifromness: The quality or state of being uniform; uniformity.
unideaed: Having no ideas; senseless; frivolous. "Unideaed girls." Mrs. Hemans. He [Bacon] received the unideaed page [Villiers] into his intimacy. Lord Campbell.
unmonopolize: To recover or release from the state of being monopolized. Unmonopolizing the rewards of learning and industry. Milton.
unneighborly: Not neighborly; distant; reserved; solitary; exclusive. -- adv. Not in a neighborly manner. Shak.
unsex: To deprive of sex, or of qualities becoming to one's sex; esp., to make unfeminine in character, manners, duties, or the like; as, to unsex a woman.
unread: 1. Not read or perused; as, an unread book. Hooker. 2. Not versed in literature; illiterate. Dryden.
unborrowed: Not borrowed; being one's own; native; original.
undeserver: One of no merit; one who is nor deserving or worthy. (old) Shak.
uncouple: To loose, as dogs, from their couples; also, to set loose; to disconnect; to disjoin; as, to uncouple railroad cars. | To roam at liberty. (old) Chaucer.
unmantle: To divest of a mantle; to uncover. Nay, she said, but I will unmantle you. Sir W. Scott.
underleaf: A prolific sort of apple, good for cider. (old) Mortimer.
unstep: To remove, as a mast, from its step.
unallied: Not allied; having no ally; having no connection or relation; as, unallied species or genera.
unwary: 1. Not vigilant against danger; not wary or cautious; unguarded; precipitate; heedless; careless. 2. Unexpected; unforeseen; unware. (old) Spenser.
unmasterable: Incapable of being mastered or subdued. (old) Sir T. Browne.
underpull: To exert one's influence secretly. (old) Ld. North.
undergown: A gown worn under another, or under some other article of dress. An undergown and kirtle of pale sea-green silk. Sir W. Scott.
unabridged: Not abridged, or shortened; full; complete; entire; whole.
unrip: To rip; to cut open. Bacon.
unifier: One who, or that which, unifies; as, a natural law is a unifier of phenomena.
unclinch: To cause to be no longer clinched; to open; as, to unclinch the fist. [Written also unclench.]
unremembrance: Want of remembrance; forgetfulness. I. Watts.
unpriced: Not priced; being without a fixed or certain value; also, priceless. "Amethyst unpriced." Neale (Rhythm of St. Bernard).
unpack: 1. To separate and remove, as things packed; to open and remove the contents of; as, to unpack a trunk. 2. To relieve of a pack or burden. Shak.
underling: An inferior person or agent; a subordinate; hence, a mean, sorry fellow. Milton. he fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, But in ourselves, that we are underlings. Shak.
unadulterate: Not adulterated; pure. "Unadulterate air." Cowper. -- Un`a*dul"ter*ate*ly, adv.
unbegot: Not begot; not yet generated; also, having never been generated; self-existent; eternal.
unicentral: Having a single center of growth. Unicentral development, that form of development which takes place primarily around a single central point, as in the lowest of unicellular organisms.
unmoor: (a) To cause to ride with one anchor less than before, after having been moored by two or more anchors. (b) To loose from anchorage. See Moor, v. t. | To weigh anchor. Sir W. Scott.
unaboat: The English name for a catboat; -- so called because Una was the name of the first boat of this kind taken to England. D. Kemp.
unfilial: Unsuitable to a son or a daughter; undutiful; not becoming a child. -- Un*fil"ial*ly, adv.
unclew: To unwind, unfold, or untie; hence, to undo; to ruin. Shak.
unclothe: To strip of clothes or covering; to make naked. I. Watts. [We] do groan being burdened; not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon. 2 Cor. v. 4.
uncontinent: Not continent; incontinent. Wyclif (2 Tim. iii. 3).
underworker: 1. One who underworks. 2. An inferior or subordinate workman. Waterland.
unbehovely: Not behooving or becoming; unseemly. [Obs. & R.] Gower.
undispensed: 1. Not dispensed. 2. Not freed by dispensation. Tooker.
unhallow: To profane; to desecrate. The vanity unhallows the virtue. L'Estrange.
unhat: To take off the hat of; to remove one's hat, especially as a mark of respect. H. Spenser.
underchamberlain: A deputy chamberlain of the exchequer.
unanimity: The quality or state of being unanimous.
unbrace: To free from tension; to relax; to loose; as, to unbrace a drum; to unbrace the nerves. Spenser.
unvalued: 1. Not valued; not appraised; hence, not considered; disregarded; valueless; as, an unvalued estate. "Unvalued persons." Shak. 2. Having inestimable value; invaluable. (old) The golden apples of unvalued price. Spenser.
untack: To separate, as what is tacked; to disjoin; to release. being untacked from honest cares. Barrow.
unify: To cause to be one; to make into a unit; to unite; to view as one. A comprehensive or unifying act of the judging faculty. De Quincey. Perception is thus a unifying act. Sir W. Hamilton.
unfailing: Not failing; not liable to fail; inexhaustible; certain; sure. Dryden. -- Un*fail"ing*ly, adv. -- Un*fail"ing*ness, n.
unfence: To strip of a fence; to remove a fence from.
unrestraint: Freedom from restraint; freedom; liberty; license.
unhoard: To take or steal from a hoard; to pilfer. Milton.
ungowned: 1. Etym: [1 st pref. un- + gown.] Stripped of a gown; unfrocked. 2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + gowned.] Not having, or not wearing, a gown.
unmerciful: Not merciful; indisposed to mercy or grace; cruel; inhuman; merciless; unkind. -- Un*mer"ci*ful*ly, adv. -- Un*mer"ci*ful*ness, n.
unprince: To deprive of the character or authority of a prince; to divest of principality of sovereignty. Swift.
unbegun: Not yet begun; also, existing without a beginning.
undeterminate: Nor determinate; not settled or certain; indeterminate. South. -- Un`de*ter"mi*nate*ness, n. Dr. H. More.
unline: To take the lining out of; hence, to empty; as, to unline one's purse.
unibranchiate: Having but one gill, as certain molluscs.
unimproved: 1. Not improved; not made better or wiser; not advanced in knowledge, manners, or excellence. 2. Not used; not employed; especially, not used or employed for a valuable purpose; as, unimproved opportunities; unimproved blessings. Cowper. 3. Not tilled, cultivated, or built upon; yielding no revenue; as, unimproved land or soil.
underlet: 1. To let below the value. All my farms were underlet. Smollett. 2. To let or lease at second hand; to sublet.
unpromise: To revoke or annul, as a promise. Chapman.
unmoved: Not moved; fixed; firm; unshaken; calm; apathetic. -- Un*mov"ed*ly, adv.
unkindred: Not kindred; not of the same kin. (old) Rowe. -- Un*kin"dred*ly, a.
unfriended: Wanting friends; not befriended; not countenanced or supported. Goldsmith. If Richard indeed does come back, it must be alone, unfollowed, unfriended. Sir W. Scott.
unseemly: Not seemly; unbecoming; indecent. An unseemly outbreak of temper. Hawthorne.
unqualitied: Deprived of the usual faculties. (old) Shak.
unweighed: Not weighed; not pondered or considered; as, an unweighed statement.
uncle: 1. The brother of one's father or mother; also applied to an aunt's husband; -- the correlative of aunt in sex, and of nephew and niece in relationship. 2. A pawnbroker. [Slang] Thackeray. My uncle, a pawnbroker. [Slang] - - Uncle Sam, a humorous appellation given to the United States Government. See Uncle Sam, in Dictionary of Noted Names in Fiction.
unpleaded: 1. Not used as a plea; not urged; as, an unpleaded excuse. 2. Not supported by pleas; undefended; as, an unpleaded suit.
unbloody: Not bloody. Dryden. Unbloody sacrifice. (a) A sacrifice in which no victim is slain. (b) (R. C. Ch.) The Mass.
unload: 1. To take the load from; to discharge of a load or cargo; to disburden; as, to unload a ship; to unload a beast. 2. Hence, to relieve from anything onerous. 3. To discharge or remove, as a load or a… | To perform the act of unloading anything; as, let unload now.
unsoul: To deprive of soul, spirit, or principle. Shelton.
unknown: Not known; not apprehended. -- Un*known"ness, n. Camden.
undulary: Moving like waves; undulatory. (old) Sir T. Browne.
underdo: To do less than is requisite or proper; -- opposed to overdo. Grew. | To do less thoroughly than is requisite; specifically, to cook insufficiently; as, to underdo the meat; -- opposed to overdo.
unfasten: To loose; to unfix; to unbind; to untie.
unvicar: To deprive of the position or office a vicar. Strype.
unlock: 1. To unfasten, as what is locked; as, to unlock a door or a chest. 2. To open, in general; to lay open; to undo. Unlock your springs, and open all your shades. Pope. [Lord] unlock the spell of sin. J. H. Newman.
unpeople: To deprive of inhabitants; to depopulate. Shak.
undevil: To free from possession by a devil or evil spirit; to exorcise. (old) They boy having gotten a habit of counterfeiting . . . would not be undeviled by all their exorcisms. Fuller.
unbe: To cause not to be; to cause to be another. [Obs. & R.] How oft, with danger of the field beset, Or with home mutinies, would he unbe Himself! Old Pay.
uniquity: The quality or state of being unique; uniqueness. Walpole.
unconstitutional: Not constitutional; not according to, or consistent with, the terms of a constitution of government; contrary to the constitution; as, an unconstitutional law, or act of an officer. Burke. -- Un*con`sti*tu"tion*al"i*ty, n. -- Un*con`sti*tu"tion*al-ly, adv.
undershapen: Under the usual shape or size; small; dwarfish. (poetic) His dwarf, a vicious undershapen thing. Tennyson.
unthread: 1. To draw or take out a thread from; as, to unthread a needle. 2. To deprive of ligaments; to loose the ligaments of. He with his bare wand can unthread thy joints. Milton. 3. To make one's way through; to traverse; as, to unthread a devious path. De Quincey.
unwellness: , n. Quality or state of being unwell.
unchristianness: The quality or state of being unchristian. Eikon Basilike.
unlearn: 1. To forget, as what has been learned; to lose from memory; also, to learn the contrary of. I had learned nothing right; I had to unlearn everything. Milner. 2. To fail to learn. (old) Dr. H. More.
unaware: Not aware; not noticing; giving no heed; thoughtless; inattentive. Swift.
untime: An unseasonable time. (old) A man shall not eat in untime. Chaucer.
unalloyed: Not alloyed; not reduced by foreign admixture; unmixed; unqualified; pure; as, unalloyed metals; unalloyed happiness. I enjoyed unalloyed satisfaction in his company. Mitford.
unbias: To free from bias or prejudice. Swift.
unwilled: Deprived of the faculty of will or volition. Mrs. Browning.
unitarianize: To change or turn to Unitarian views.
undeaf: To free from deafness; to cause to hear. (old) Shak.
unblindfold: To free from that which blindfolds. Spenser.
uncanonize: 1. To deprive of canonical authority. 2. To reduce from the rank of a canonized saint.
unbreech: 1. To remove the breeches of; to divest or strip of breeches. Shak. 2. (Gun.) To free the breech of, as a cannon, from its fastenings or coverings. Pennant.
unconcern: Want of concern; absence of anxiety; freedom from solicitude; indifference. A listless unconcern, Cold, and averting from our neighbor's good. Thomson.
unscience: Want of science or knowledge; ignorance. (old) If that any wight ween a thing to be otherwise than it is, it is not only unscience, but it is deceivable opinion. Chaucer.
unanswered: 1. Not answered; not replied; as, an unanswered letter. 2. Not refuted; as, an unanswered argument. 3. Not responded to in kind; unrequited; as, unanswered affection.
unwish: To wish not to be; to destroy by wishing. (old) Now thou hast unwished five thousand men. Shak.
underwood: Small trees and bushes that grow among large trees; coppice; underbrush; -- formerly used in the plural. Shrubs and underwoods look well enough while they grow within the shade of oaks and cedars. Addison.
unspar: To take the spars, stakes, or bars from. Sir W. Scott.
underget: To get under or beneath; also, to understand. (old) R. of Gloucester.
unless: Upon any less condition than (the fact or thing stated in the sentence or clause which follows); if not; supposing that not; if it be not; were it not that; except; as, we shall fail unless we are industrious.
unsociable: Not sociable; not inclined to society; averse to companionship or conversation; solitary; reserved; as, an unsociable person or temper. -- Un*so"cia*ble*ness, n. -- Un*so"cia*bly, adv.
unframe: To take apart, or destroy the frame of. Dryden.
unsafety: The quality or state of being in peril; absence of safety; insecurity. Bacon.
unreasonable: Not reasonable; irrational; immoderate; exorbitant. -- Un*rea"son*a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*rea"son*a*bly, adv.
unspecialized: Not specialized; specifically (Biol.), not adapted, or set apart, for any particular purpose or function; as, an unspecialized unicellular organism. W. K. Brooks.
undercliff: A subordinate cliff on a shore, consisting of material that has fallen from the higher cliff above.
understandingly: In an understanding manner; intelligibly; with full knowledge or comprehension; intelligently; as, to vote upon a question understandingly; to act or judge understandingly. The gospel may be neglected, but in can not be understandingly disbelieved. J. Hawes.
unpoised: 1. Not poised or balanced. 2. Not poised or weighed; hence, regardless of consequences; unhesitating. (old) Marston.
unisexual: Having one sex only, as plants which have the male and female flowers on separate individuals, or animals in which the sexes are in separate individuals; dioecious; -- distinguished from bisexual, or hermaphrodite. See Dioecious.
unwayed: 1. Not used to travel; as, colts that are unwayed. (old) Suckling. 2. Having no ways or roads; pathless. (old) Wyclif.
unthink: To recall or take back, as something thought. Shak.
unflinching: Not flinching or shrinking; unyielding. -- Un*flinch"ing*ly, adv.
underskirt: A petticoat; the foundation skirt of a draped dress.
unbank: To remove a bank from; to open by, or as if by, the removal of a bank. H. Taylor.
unkindly: 1. Not kindly; unkind; ungracious. 2. Unnatural; contrary to nature. (old) "Unkindly crime." Spenser. 3. Unfavorable; annoying; malignant. Milton.
unideal: 1. Not ideal; real; unimaginative. 2. Unideaed. Johnson.
unburrow: To force from a burrow; to unearth.
universal: 1. Of or pertaining to the universe; extending to, including, or affecting, the whole number, quantity, or space; unlimited; general; all-reaching; all-pervading; as, universal ruin; universal good; | 1. The whole; the general system of the universe; the universe. (old) Plato calleth God the cause and original, the nature and reason, of the universal. Sir W. Raleigh. 2.
undeeded: 1. Not deeded or transferred by deed; as, undeeded land. 2. Not made famous by any great action. (old) Shak.
unoriginated: 1. Not originated; existing from all eternity. F. W. Newman. 2. Not yet caused to be, or to be made; as, possible inventions still unoriginated.
unfalcated: 1. Not falcated, or hooked. 2. Having no deductions; not curtailed, or shortened; undiminished. Swift.
uniform: 1. Having always the same form, manner, or degree; not varying or variable; unchanging; consistent; equable; homogenous; as, the dress of the Asiatics has been uniform from early ages; | A dress of a particular style or fashion worn by persons in the same service or order by means of which they have a distinctive appearance; as, the uniform of the artillery, of the police, of the…
unextricable: Not extricable; inextricable. (old) Dr. H. More.
uniflorous: Bearing one flower only; as, a uniflorous peduncle.
unproper: Not proper or peculiar; improper. (old) -- Un*prop"er*ly, adv. (old)
unprovide: To deprive of necessary provision; to unfurnish. Lest her . . . beauty unprovide my mind again. Shak.
unhand: To loose from the hand; to let go. Hold off! unhand me, gray beard loon! Eftsoons his hand dropped he. Coleridge.
unstock: 1. To deprive of a stock; to remove the stock from; to loose from that which fixes, or holds fast. 2. To remove from the stocks, as a ship.
unregeneracy: The quality or state of being unregenerate. Glanvill.
unweighing: Not weighing or pondering; inconsiderate. Shak.
underyoke: To subject to the yoke; to make subject. Wyclif.
unliken: To make unlike; to dissimilate. (old) Wyclif.
undaunted: Not daunted; not subdued or depressed by fear. Shak. Syn. -- Bold; fearless; brave; courageous; intrepid. -- Un*daunt"ed*ly, adv. -- Un*daunt"ed*ness, n.
unloose: To make loose; to loosen; to set free. Shak. | To become unfastened; to lose all connection or union.
unbuckle: To loose the buckles of; to unfasten; as, to unbuckle a shoe. "Unbuckle anon thy purse." Chaucer.
understudy: To study, as another actor's part, in order to be his substitute in an emergency; to study another actor's part. | One who studies another's part with a view to assuming it in an emergency.
untenant: To remove a tenant from. Coleridge.
unedge: To deprive of the edge; to blunt. J. Fletcher.
undersleeve: A sleeve of an under-garment; a sleeve worn under another,
unwonted: 1. Not wonted; unaccustomed; unused; not made familiar by practice; as, a child unwonted to strangers. Milton. 2. Uncommon; unusual; infrequent; rare; as, unwonted changes. "Unwonted lights." Byron. -- Un*wont"ed*ly, adv. -- Un*wont"ed*ness, n.
unlikeliness: The quality or state of being unlikely.
underside: The lower or lowest side of anything. Paley.
ungulata: An extensive group of mammals including all those that have hoofs. It comprises the Artiodactyla and Perissodactyla.
unclosed: 1. Not separated by inclosures; open. Clarendon. 2. Not finished; not concluded. Madison. 3. Not closed; not sealed; open. Byron.
underdealing: Crafty, unfair, or underhand dealing; unfair practice; trickery. Milton.
unleash: To free from a leash, or as from a leash; to let go; to release; as, to unleash dogs.
uneath: Not easy; difficult; hard. (old) Who he was, uneath was to descry. Spenser. | Not easily; hardly; scarcely. (old) Uneath may she endure the flinty streets. Shak.
unseel: To open, as the eyes of a hawk that have been seeled; hence, to give light to; to enlighten. (old) B. Jonson.
unsuit: Not to suit; to be unfit for. (old) Quarles.
unconcerned: Not concerned; not anxious or solicitous; easy in mind; carelessly secure; indifferent; as, to be unconcerned at what has happened; to be unconcerned about the future. -- Un`con*cern"ed*ly, adv. -- Un`con*cern"ed*ness, n. Happy mortals, unconcerned for more. Dryden.
uniformitarian: Of, pertaining to, or designating, the view or doctrine that existing causes, acting in the same manner and with essentially the same intensity as at the present time, are sufficient to account for… | One who accepts uniformitarianism, or the uniformitarian doctrine.
undersized: Of a size less than is common.
ungeld: A person so far out of the protection of the law, that if he were murdered, no geld, or fine, should be paid, or composition made by him that killed him. Cowell. Burrill.
unbless: To deprive of blessings; to make wretched. (old) Shak.
undecked: 1. Not decked; unadorned. [Eve] undecked, save with herself, more lovely fair. Milton. 2. Not having a deck; as, an undecked vessel.
unwemmed: Not blemished; undefiled; pure. (old) Wyclif. With body clean and with unwemmed thought. Chaucer.
unbenumb: To relieve of numbness; to restore sensation to.
unresisted: 1. Not resisted; unopposed. Bentley. 2. Resistless; as, unresisted fate. Pope.
untraveled: 1. Not traveled; not trodden by passengers; as, an untraveled forest. 2. Having never visited foreign countries; not having gained knowledge or experience by travel; as, an untraveled Englishman. Addison.
unmask: To strip of a mask or disguise; to lay open; to expose.
unguard: To deprive of a guard; to leave unprotected. Sterne.
unpower: Want of power; weakness. (old) Piers Plowman.
universalness: The quality or state of being universal; universality.
unsheathe: To deprive of a sheath; to draw from the sheath or scabbard, as a sword. To unsheathe the sword, to make war.
ungraceful: Not graceful; not marked with ease and dignity; deficient in beauty and elegance; inelegant; awkward; as, ungraceful manners; ungraceful speech. The other oak remaining a blackened and ungraceful trunk. Sir W. Scott. -- Un*grace"ful*ly, adv. -- Un*grace"ful*ness, n.
unguis: 1. The nail, claw, talon, or hoof of a finger, toe, or other appendage. 2. (Zoöl.) One of the terminal hooks on the foot of an insect. 3. (Bot.) The slender base of a petal in some flowers; a claw; called also ungula.
unattached: 1. Not attached; not adhering; having no engagement; free. 2. (Mil.) Not assigned to any company or regiment. 3. (Law) Not taken or arrested. R. Junius.
unsettledness: The quality or state of being unsettled.
unwilling: Not willing; loath; disinclined; reluctant; as, an unwilling servant. And drop at last, but in unwilling ears, This saving counsel, "Keep your piece nine years." Pope. -- Un*will"ing*ly, adv. -- Un*will"ing*ness, n.
unassented: Not assented; -- said specif. of stocks or bonds the holders of which refuse to deposit them by way of assent to an agreement altering their status, as in a readjustment.
unbone: 1. To deprive of bones, as meat; to bone. 2. To twist about, as if boneless. Milton.
undergrowth: That which grows under trees; specifically, shrubs or small trees growing among large trees. Milton.
unwont: Unwonted; unused; unaccustomed. (old) Sir W. Scott.
unseconded: 1. Not seconded; not supported, aided, or assisted; as, the motion was unseconded; the attempt was unseconded. 2. Not exemplified a second time. (old) "Strange and unseconded shapes of worms." Sir T. Browne.
unfeudalize: To free from feudal customs or character; to make not feudal. Carlyle.
unconformability: 1. The quality or state of being unconformable; unconformableness. 2. (Geol.) Want of parallelism between one series of strata and another, especially when due to a disturbance of the position of the earlier strata before the latter were deposited.
undercharge: 1. To charge below or under; to charge less than is usual or suitable fro; as, to undercharge goods or services. 2. To put too small a charge into; as, to undercharge a gun. | A charge that is less than is usual or suitable.
unchristianize: To turn from the Christian faith; to cause to abandon the belief and profession of Christianity.
uniseptate: Having but one septum, or partition; -- said of two-celled fruits, such as the silicles of cruciferous plants.
uncrown: To deprive of a crown; to take the crown from; hence, to discrown; to dethrone. He hath done me wrong, And therefore I'll uncrown him ere't be long. Shak.
unreliable: Not reliable; untrustworthy. See Reliable. -- Un`re*li"a*ble*ness, n. Alcibiades . . . was too unsteady, and (according to Mr. Coleridge's coinage) "unreliable;" or perhaps, in more correct English, too "unrelyuponable." De Quincey.
unfetter: To loose from fetters or from restraint; to unchain; to unshackle; to liberate; as, to unfetter the mind.
unhood: To remove a hood or disguise from. Quarterly Rev.
unipara: A woman who has borne one child.
unbay: To free from the restraint of anything that surrounds or incloses; to let loose; to open. (old) I ought . . . to unbay the current of my passion. Norris.
uncharitable: Not charitable; contrary to charity; severe in judging; harsh; censorious; as, uncharitable opinions or zeal. Addison. -- Un*char"i*ta*ble*ness, n. -- Un*char"i*ta*bly, adv.
unmorrised: Not arrayed in the dress of a morris dancer. (old) Beau. & Fl.
ungored: Not stained with gore; not bloodied. Sylvester.
univocal: 1. Having one meaning only; -- contrasted with equivocal. 2. Having unison of sound, as the octave in music. See Unison, n., 2. 3. Having always the same drift or tenor; uniform; certain; regular. | 1. (Aristotelian Logic) A generic term, or a term applicable in the same sense to all the species it embraces. 2. A word having but one meaning.
underfilling: The filling below or beneath; the under part of a building. Sir H. Wotton.
unclutch: 1. To open, as something closely shut. "Unclutch his griping hand." Dr. H. More. 2. (Mech.) To disengage, as a clutch.
untraded: 1. Not dealt with in trade; not visited for purposes of trade. (old) Hakluyt 2. Unpracticed; inexperienced. (old) Udall. 3. Not traded in or bartered; hence, not hackneyed; unusual; not common. Shak.
undergrow: To grow to an inferior, or less than the usual, size or height. Wyclif.
unigenous: Being of one kind; being of the same genus.
underlocker: A person who inspects a mine daily; -- called also underviewer.
unveil: To remove a veil from; to divest of a veil; to uncover; to disclose to view; to reveal; as, she unveiled her face. | To remove a veil; to reveal one's self.
unpolite: Not polite; impolite; rude. -- Un`po*lite"ly, adv. -- Un`po*lite"ness, n.
unwill: To annul or reverse by an act of the will. Longfellow.
unbroken: Not broken; continuous; unsubdued; as, an unbroken colt.
uniformism: The doctrine of uniformity in the geological history of the earth; -- in part equivalent to uniformitarianism, but also used, more broadly, as opposed to catastrophism.
unhelmed: 1. Etym: [Properly p. p. of unhelm.] Divested or deprived of the helm or helmet. 2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + helm.] Not wearing a helmet; without a helmet. Sir W. Scott.
uncowl: To divest or deprive of a cowl. Pope.
underlay: 1. To lay beneath; to put under. 2. To raise or support by something laid under; as, to underlay a cut, plate, or the like, for printing. See Underlay, n., 2. 3. To put a tap on (a shoe). [Prov. Eng.] | To incline from the vertical; to hade; -- said of a vein, fault, or lode.
undress: 1. To divest of clothes; to strip. 2. To divest of ornaments to disrobe. 3. (Med.) To take the dressing, or covering, from; as, to undress a wound. | 1. A loose, negligent dress; ordinary dress, as distinguished from full dress. 2. (Mil. & Naval) An authorized habitual dress of officers and soldiers, but not full-dress uniform.
unskillful: 1. Not skillful; inexperienced; awkward; bungling; as, an unskillful surgeon or mechanic; an unskillful logician. 2. Lacking discernment; injudicious; ignorant. Though it make the unskillful laugh, can not but make the judicious grieve. Shak. -- Un*skill"ful*ly, adv. -- Un*skill"ful*ness, n.
unlaid: 1. Not laid or placed; not fixed. Hooker. 2. Not allayed; not pacified; not laid finally to rest. "Stubborn, unlaid ghost." Milton. 3. Not laid out, as a corpse. B. Jonson. Unlaid paper. See Laid paper, under Laid.
unbridle: To free from the bridle; to set loose.
unpedigreed: Not distinguished by a pedigree. Pollok.
unfix: 1. To loosen from a fastening; to detach from anything that holds; to unsettle; as, to unfix a bayonet; to unfix the mind or affections. 2. To make fluid; to dissolve. The mountain stands; nor can the rising sun Unfix her frosts. Dryden.
unholy: Not holy; unhallowed; not consecrated; hence, profane; wicked; impious. -- Un*ho"li*ly, adv. -- Un*ho"li*ness, n.
unmoralized: Not restrained or tutored by morality. Norris.
unbewitch: To free from a spell; to disenchant. South.
unauthorize: To disown the authority of; to repudiate.
unimplicate: Not implicated. "Unimplicate in folly." R. Browning.
untuck: To unfold or undo, as a tuck; to release from a tuck or fold.
undertow: The current that sets seaward near the bottom when waves are breaking upon the shore.
unshelve: To remove from, or as from, a shelf.
unconsecrate: To render not sacred; to deprive of sanctity; to desecrate. (old) South.
unseen: 1. Not seen or discovered. 2. Unskilled; inexperienced. (old) Clarendon.
unplumb: To deprive of lead, as of a leaden coffin. Burke.
underwrite: 1. To write under something else; to subscribe. What addition and change I have made I have here underwritten. Bp. Sanderson. 2. To subscribe one's name to for insurance, especially for marine… | To practice the business of insuring; to take a risk of insurance on a vessel or the like.
unstate: To deprive of state or dignity. High-battled Cæsar will unstate his happiness. Shak.
unwit: To deprive of wit. (old) Shak. | Want of wit or understanding; ignorance. (old) Chaucer.
unguentary: Like an unguent, or partaking of its qualities.
unoperculated: Destitute of an operculum, or cover.
unswell: To sink from a swollen state; to subside. (old) Chaucer.
unionistic: Of or pertaining to union or unionists; tending to promote or preserve union.
unfoldment: The acct of unfolding, or the state of being unfolded. The extreme unfoldment of the instinctive powers. C. Morris.
unbend: 1. To free from flexure; to make, or allow to become, straight; to loosen; as, to unbend a bow. 2. A remit from a strain or from exertion; to set at ease for a time; to relax; | 1. To cease to be bent; to become straight or relaxed. 2. To relax in exertion, attention, severity, or the like; hence, to indulge in mirth or amusement.
unromanized: 1. Not subjected to Roman arms or customs. J. Whitaker. 2. (Eccl.) Not subjected to the principles or usages of the Roman Catholic Church.
unhap: Ill luck; misfortune. (old) "The cause of her unhap." Sir P. Sidney.
underlie: 1. To lie under; to rest beneath; to be situated under; as, a stratum of clay underlies the surface gravel. 2. To be at the basis of; to form the foundation of; to support; as, a doctrine underlying a theory. 3. To be subject or amenable to. The knight of Ivanhoe . . . underlies the challenge of Brian der Bois Guilbert. Sir W. Scott.
undergird: To blind below; to gird round the bottom. They used helps, undergirding the ship. Acts xxvii. 17.
underspore: To raise with a spar, or piece of wood, used as a lever. (old) Give me a staff that I may underspore. Chaucer.
unliquored: 1. Not moistened or wet with liquor; dry. "Unliquored coach." Bp. Hall. 2. Not in liquor; not intoxicated; sober. Like an unliquored Silenus. Milton.
unshale: To strip the shale, or husk, from; to uncover. (old) I will not unshale the jest before it be ripe. Marston.
unpick: To pick out; to undo by picking.
unchild: 1. To bereave of children; to make childless. Shak. 2. To make unlike a child; to divest of the characteristics of a child. Bp. Hall.
uncape: To remove a cap or cape from. (old)
unroll: 1. To open, as what is rolled or convolved; as, to unroll cloth; to unroll a banner. 2. To display; to reveal. Dryden. 3. To remove from a roll or register, as a name. If I make not this cheat bring out another . . . let me be unrolled and my name put in the book of virtue! Shak.
ungula: 1. A hoof, claw, or talon. 2. (Geom.) A section or part of a cylinder, cone, or other solid of revolution, cut off by a plane oblique to the base; -- so called from its resemblance to the hoof of a horse. 3. (Bot.) Same as Unguis, 3. Spherical ungula (Geom.), a part of a sphere bounded by two planes intersecting in a diameter and by a line of the surface of the sphere.
undirect: To misdirect; to mislead. (old) who make false fires to undirect seamen in a tempest. Fuller.
undershrievalty: The office or position of an undersheriff.
ungentle: Not gentle; lacking good breeding or delicacy; harsh. Vicious, ungentle, foolish, blunt, unkind. Shak. That ungentle flavor which distinguishes nearly all our native and uncultivated grapes. Hawthorne. -- Un*gen"tle*ness, n. -- Un*gen"tly, adv.
uncommon: Not common; unusual; infrequent; rare; hence, remarkable; strange; as, an uncommon season; an uncommon degree of cold or heat; uncommon courage. Syn. -- Rare; scarce; infrequent; unwonted. -- Un*com"mon*ly, adv. -- Un*com"mon*ness, n.
uncapper: An instrument for removing an explode cap from a cartridge shell.
underhead: A blockhead, or stupid person; a dunderhead. (old) Sir T. Browne.
underloadswitch: A switch which opens a circuit when the current falls below a certain predetermined value, used to protect certain types of motors from running at excessive speed upon decrease of load.
unpersuasion: The state of not being persuaded; disbelief; doubt. Abp. Leighton.
unwonder: To divest of the quality of wonder or mystery; to interpret; to explain. Fuller.
undreamt: Not dreamed, or dreamed of; not thof. Unpathed waters, undreamed shores. Shak.
unhoop: To strip or deprive of hoops; to take away the hoops of.
united: Combined; joined; made one. United Brethren. (Eccl.) See Moravian, n. -- United flowers (Bot.), flowers which have the stamens and pistils in the same flower. -- The United Kingdom, Great Britain and Ireland; -- so named since January 1, 1801, when the Legislative Union went into operation.
uniplicate: Having, or consisting of, but one fold.
unregenerated: Not regenerated; not renewed in heart; remaining or being at enmity with God.
unplat: To take out the folds or twists of, as something previously platted; to unfold; to unwreathe.
underpossessor: One who possesses or holds anything subject to the superior of another. Jer. Taylor.
unimuscular: Having only one adductor muscle, and one muscular impression on each valve, as the oyster; monomyarian.
unlord: To deprive of the rank or position of a lord. Milton.
unchariot: To throw out of a chariot. Pope.
unloader: One who, or that which, unloads; a device for unloading, as hay from a wagon.
uncap: To remove a cap or cover from.
understander: One who understands, or knows by experience. Dryden.
unclean: 1. Not clean; foul; dirty; filthy. 2. Ceremonially impure; needing ritual cleansing. He that toucheth the dead body of any man shall be unclean seven days. Num. xix. 11. 3. Morally impure. "Adultery of the heart, consisting of inordinate and unclean affections." Perkins. -- Un*clean"ly, adv. -- Un*clean"ness, n.
unpoison: To remove or expel poison from. (old) South.
unhinge: 1. To take from the hinges; as, to unhinge a door. 2. To displace; to unfix by violence. Blackmore. 3. To render unstable or wavering; to unsettle; as, to unhinge one's mind or opinions; to unhinge the nerves. Why should I then unhinge my brains, ruin my mind South. His sufferings, nay the revolutions of his fate, had not in the least unhinged his mind. Walpole.
uniter: One who, or that which, unites.
undulative: Consisting in, or accompanied by, undulations; undulatory.
uncloister: To release from a cloister, or from confinement or seclusion; to set free; to liberate.
